articles.title: Prosecutors allege long-running scheme to raise money for Hamas
articles.summary: Two brothers are among those arrested and accused of falsely soliciting donations for “the poor and orphans in Gaza” via social media, court records show.
articles.body: A purported media representative for Hamas has been accused of funneling roughly $1.7 million to the terrorist organization from donors in the U.S. and elsewhere who believed they were giving humanitarian aid to Gaza, according to a federal indictment unsealed Thursday. Saleem Alzaq was indicted by a federal grand jury in New York and was charged with money laundering and violating sanctions, according to the charging document. He was believed to be in Gaza. Two brothers in the U.S. were also charged in connection with the long-running scheme to raise money for Hamas, by disseminating propaganda and soliciting donations for “the poor and orphans in Gaza” via social media, court records show. Abdel Adhami and Omar Adhami were arrested last month in Louisiana, but the details of their charges were unsealed only after they made their first court appearances, court dockets show. Abdel Adhami faces charges of material support to a foreign terrorist organization, wire fraud and money laundering, according to a complaint filed on Sept. 11 in the Eastern District of Louisiana. Meanwhile, his brother Omar Adhami is also charged with material support and wire fraud charges, according to his complaint. An attorney for the brothers didn’t immediately return a call seeking comment. They were detained pending a detention hearing and have not yet entered a plea. From 2021 to November 2025, Abdel Adhami used various Snapchat accounts to post Hamas propaganda and raise money for the terrorist organization after referring social media followers to his Telegram account, according to his criminal complaint. Abdel Adhami also allegedly solicited money for Gaza through Instagram. All told, from Nov. 4, 2023, to June 2025, Abdel Adhami sent almost $35,000 to one PayPal account and $46,600 to another PayPal account, the complaint states. The money was funneled to Alzaq, according to the complaint. Investigators were able to identify Abdel Adhami as the source of those funds last year, after an NYPD online covert officer reached out to Alzaq. Alzaq, in turn, unwittingly referred the covert NYPD officer back to Abdel Adhami, the complaint states. “This is the message I wanted to deliver to the person who donated the bread,” Alzaq said around Jan. 28, 2024, in a voice message to a Snapchat account controlled by Abdel Adhami, according to the court papers. “Some of them received the bread, thanks be to God.” In his complaint, investigators said Omar Adhami also sent Alzaq some $3,000 and on one occasion requested “to have a sheep or goat slaughtered for the needy and poor in Gaza.” New York Police Department Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Thursday in a statement that the NYPD’s “counterterrorism work knows no borders. Our intelligence analysts uncovered this international finance network and built the case.”

articles.title: 'Potential crime' probe into death of Scots wingsuit flyer dropped
articles.summary: British champion Liam Byrne, 24, was fatally injured on the Gitschen mountain in June last year.
articles.body:
An investigation into any potential crime after the death of a Scottish wingsuit flyer during a jump in the Swiss Alps has been dropped.

British champion Liam Byrne, 24, was fatally injured on the Gitschen mountain after taking off from 7,874ft (2,400m) in June last year.

An investigation was launched, but documents from the Swiss Federal Prosecutor's Office seen by BBC Scotland News show it was decided to discontinue proceedings.

Byrne, from Stonehaven, Aberdeenshire, had featured in a 2024 BBC documentary called The Boy Who Can Fly .

He was described as a very experienced wingsuit flyer - which is a type of skydiving. It involves wearing a special suit with webbing to allow mid-air lift.

Byrne had completed thousands of jumps during his flying career.

Scottish wingsuit flyer Liam Byrne dies during Swiss Alps jump

He had told the BBC documentary: "I think I was about 13 when I said to my dad that I wanted to learn to fly like a bird."

He took to extreme sports from a young age.

At 12 he climbed Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest peak standing at 19,341ft (5,895 metres) high.

That adventure led to dog-sledging through the Arctic, scuba diving, and multiple high summit climbs.

By the age of 14 he was a licensed paraglider.

He did his first skydive aged 16, and by 18 was pulling on a wingsuit, which he described as a "second skin, letting me move through the air in a controlled way".

The Swiss Federal Prosecutor's Office report on the decision to discontinue the investigation said the first two wingsuit jumpers in the party landed without incident.

However, it said Byrne collided with the mountainside and suffered fatal injuries.

The report said proceedings would be discontinued if there was insufficient evidence of any criminal suspicion, such as knowingly placing life in danger.

"The fatal crash was, with a high degree of probability, attributable to a situation from which there was no escape, resulting from insufficient lift and the low altitude above the ground," it said.

"There are no indications in the present case of any criminal acts by third parties that contributed to the crash, or of a pre-existing technical defect in the equipment used that contributed to the crash.

"The proceedings are therefore discontinued."

A family statement at the time of his death said: "We would like to remember Liam not just for the way he left this world, but for how he lived in it.

"Liam was fearless, not necessarily because he wasn't afraid but because he refused to let fear hold him back.

"He chased life in a way that most of us only dream of and he soared.

"Skydiving and base jumping was more than just a thrill for Liam - it was freedom.

articles.title: First minister demands 'new deal' for Wales before Plaid Cymru conference
articles.summary: Rhun ap Iorwerth will address members at Plaid's first conference since winning the Senedd election.
articles.body:
First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth has written to the prime minister to request "a new deal for Wales" before his first Plaid Cymru conference speech since taking office.

In his letter to Andy Burnham, sent on Thursday and seen by BBC Wales, the Plaid leader called for more powers to be transferred to Cardiff.

Burnham previously said he would "give a fair hearing" to anything put to him by the Welsh first minister.

Ap Iorwerth will address party members in Llandudno on Friday, five months on from Plaid's historic success at May's Senedd election .

The result saw the party win power for the first time, ending Labour's 27 years in government since devolution began in 1999.

'Too early' to know if Burnham will back more Welsh powers, says first minister

PM rules out giving Wales independence referendum powers

However, without a majority of the seats in Cardiff Bay, ap Iorwerth leads a minority administration which has to work with opposition Members of the Senedd to pass new laws and budgets.

The government lost a key vote on its spending plans in July.

In his speech, ap Iorwerth will say the election "delivered a clear mandate from the people of Wales for positive change that makes a tangible difference to their lives".

"This mandate includes extending devolution to enable the Senedd and the Welsh government to have the necessary tools - powers, funding and financial flexibilities - to drive the maximum improvement in outcomes for the people of Wales by integrating and improving public services and growing the economy.

"As an underpinning principle to support these reforms, Wales should be able to benefit from the same constitutional and fiscal tools already available in Scotland."

Ap Iorwerth hosted the pro-independence first ministers of Scotland and Northern Ireland in Cardiff last month and jointly declared that "Westminster's time is coming to an end" .

In his 2,000-word letter to Burnham, ap Iorwerth made a detailed case for the transfer of powers over policing and justice, rail infrastructure, and the Crown Estate to Wales.

He also called for "funding arrangements that are fair, needs-based and reflect Wales' demographic and economic realities".

He said that "Wales' constitutional settlement should continue to evolve to improve democratic accountability, boost growth, strengthen public services and deliver better outcomes for our communities".

Ap Iorwerth is expected to meet the prime minister, along with the first ministers of Scotland and Northern Ireland, at the end of the month.

Burnham had previously said he would be "open" to the idea of giving the Welsh government control over policing.

He has also said : "I have to respect the governments in the nations of the UK, and I will, and give a fair hearing to anything that is put to me."

A UK government spokesperson said: "This government is committed to building a stronger and fairer Wales in a stronger and fairer United Kingdom.

"That's why our focus is now on working with the Welsh government to empower local leaders and communities to deliver good growth and jobs in every postcode."

articles.title: What are the new rules in Scotland's supermarkets?
articles.summary: Restrictions are being put on products with high sugar, fat and salt content, but the meal deal lives on.
articles.body:
Sugary soft drinks, biscuits and some breakfast cereals have disappeared from prominent positions in Scotland's supermarkets.

The Scottish government has introduced rules meaning some products that are high in fat, sugar and salt can no longer be put in prime end-of-aisle slots, or feature as part of multi-buy offers in store or online.

The regulations will apply to the usual suspects - chocolate, crisps, biscuits and ice cream.

But it could also include kombucha, seaweed snacks, muesli and chewing gum, depending on their sugar content.

The Scottish government regulations apply to businesses with more than 50 employees. This could include supermarkets, high street shops, restaurants, pharmacies, petrol stations and garden centres.

They are are no longer allowed to display pre-packaged foods including sugary soft drinks, confectionery, biscuits and breakfast cereals in prominent locations such as entrances, checkouts, aisle ends and designated queueing areas.

Price promotions on those items - such as "three for the price of two", "three for £10" or "buy five and save 20%" - are no longer allowed.

Multi-buy offers, including extra loyalty points, are also banned.

Another type of deal that falls foul of the rules is those offering a free high-sugar, fat or salt product alongside another purchase - for example, a free chocolate bar with a newspaper.

There are no restrictions on discounts such as half-price or "save £1".

Online retailers also face restrictions - including a ban on advertising some foods on their homepage.

Similar restrictions are already in place in England and Wales .

The short answer is: a lot, if there’s enough sugar, salt or fat packed into it.

Drinks with added sugar - such as lemonade, soda, squash, chocolate milk, almond milk, ready-made coffee, kombucha, energy drinks, and hot chocolate

Savoury snacks such as crisps and tortilla chips, and even lentil-based crisps and seaweed snacks, depending on their content

Breakfast cereals, granola, muesli and oat-based cereals

Pre-made pizzas, roast potatoes, chips, fish fingers and chicken nuggets

Ready meals, as well as pasta, rice or noodles with added ingredients or fillings, such as ravioli and tortellini

Confectionary, such as popcorn, chocolate, chewing gum and sweets

Ice cream, sorbets, ice lollies, sponge cakes, custard, jelly, crumbles

Cereal bars, biscuits, scones, flapjacks, doughnuts and Danish pastries

Sweetened Greek-style, probiotic, kids' and drinking yoghurts

Meal deals are exempt from the regulations, as are "dine for two" offers.

However, any foods identified in the rules, whether part of a meal deal or not, cannot be placed in the restricted locations, such as supermarket entrances.

The Scottish government regulations are being introduced to encourage healthier eating choices.

Public Health Minister Maree Todd noted that two out of three Scottish adults are overweight or obese, with those living in the poorest areas worst affected.

She said: "We know that promotions and prominent product placement can encourage over-consumption and impulse buying of foods with high levels of calories, fat, sugar and salt.

"By restricting the promotion of less healthy food and drink we can make it easier for people to make healthier choices, improving health and wellbeing, and create a Scotland where everyone eats well and has a healthy weight."

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'Laughing criminals let loose' and 'Return to the castle'
articles.summary: Inmates who were released early from prisons in England and Wales are pictured on several of Friday's front pages.
articles.body:
Spoiler warning: This press review reveals details from the first episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

The Daily Telegraph warns the UK is "at risk of fuel shortages" after President Donald Trump threatened to cut off US diesel shipments unless Europe released emergency reserves. The paper notes it is "unclear whether the UK would be directly included" in any threatened export ban, but that such a move would "rapidly increase pump prices". A Trump administration official tells the Financial Times it is "in Europe's best interests to work with the United States" to boost supply and bring down costs. A Whitehall source quoted in the Times accuses Washington of "brazen negotiating tactics" , and says reserve stocks are "there to act as a buffer against supply shortages".

The Guardian has been told that "ministers are working up sweeping plans for welfare changes". They apparently include "scrapping the health element of universal credit for under 25s" and replacing it with a "multibillion-pound package of support to get into work". The government says it will not pre-empt the findings of two reviews due in the autumn and that it will "always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable".

Sources close to Number 10 have told the i Paper that holding a snap general election in May "has not been ruled out" - despite Burnham's "insistence that there would not be one".

The Daily Mail declares Thursday's early release of prisoners in England and Wales the "first of ten tidal waves of convicts". The paper quotes a man freed from HMP Brixton as saying he is "gonna go stealing again". Another from Wandsworth Prison, on his way to "get some kebabs", says the early releases are "good" because the jail is "full".

The Sun calls Downing Street's clarification of the prime minister's position on Manchester City's dispute with the Premier League an "own goal". The paper says he was accused of "political interference" after saying he did not want to "lose" the club's owners. Number 10 has since said there cannot be "any suggestion that anyone is above the rules". City deny any wrongdoing.

articles.title: Records give insight into how one Cornell student responded to rape accusation
articles.summary: One of the seven Cornell University fraternity brothers named in a lawsuit alleging a gang rape in 2024 said he did not see the accuser in distress during his brief time in the room where she says she was sexually assaulted while she was under the influence of several substances.
articles.body: One of the seven Cornell University fraternity brothers named in a lawsuit alleging a gang rape in 2024 said he did not see the accuser in distress during his brief time in the room where she says she was sexually assaulted while she was under the influence of several substances. Scott Kretzschmar, now 22, said that after he saw a fraternity Snapchat post advertising “free p----y” upstairs, he went in the room already filled with several of his fraternity brothers — but that he never saw the woman naked, touched her or used ketamine. Kretzschmar’s accounting of the evening was laid out in court documents he filed anonymously in Tompkins County, New York, Supreme Court in March in a last-ditch effort to annul Cornell’s decision to find him responsible for attempted sexual exploitation after its Title IX investigation. In the failed petition, Kretzschmar argued that the school improperly found him responsible for an offense that was not on his original list of violations — and then denied his appeal earlier this year. The court records, together with text messages separately obtained by NBC News between Jane Doe and another Chi Phi fraternity member she later accused of assault, provide further context for the October 2024 incident and its immediate aftermath. The incident has reignited a national conversation about sexual assault and consent. “My reputation is destroyed and i’m utterly ashamed,” Jane Doe texted another fraternity member, four days after she alleges she was raped while she was under the influence of ketamine, marijuana and alcohol. “I’m f------g pissed cause this many people shouldn’t know and i feel like i know who some of the rats in the room were,” she wrote. “if i ever find out i swear to god its in sight.” During the dayslong text exchange, Jane Doe fluctuated between anger over being the subject of campus gossip and sending friendly messages before she ultimately cut off communication the day before she reported her allegations to campus police. The report spurred a university investigation of seven Chi Phi members that culminated with a 12-day internal federal civil rights proceeding known as Title IX in May 2025, at which more than 30 witnesses testified following 50 investigative interviews, according to filings in Kretzschmar’s appeal. The investigation found that the night of the alleged assault, a photo of Jane Doe was shared among active Chi Phi members in a Snapchat group, the documents revealed. The nature of the photo is not made clear in the court documents. “Are you guys at least naked?” a Snapchat message from an unknown user said after the photo was posted. The Snapchat message thread, which was provided to campus investigators anonymously, “became a key exhibit in the resulting student conduct matter,” attorneys for the university argued in a July 17 memo filed in Kretzschmar’s case. Jane Doe’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, told NBC News she learned of the Snapchat messages only when they were leaked to her by another fraternity member who was outraged by what his fraternity brothers were said to have done to her. Ultimately, the seven received differing penalties, ranging from writing a “reflection paper” to expulsion. The case went to the local district attorney’s office, which ultimately declined to bring criminal charges. Cornell University police declined to comment on whether they had the photo when they conducted the November 2024 investigation into Jane Doe’s claims. The university did not respond to a request for comment on the photo and other details reported in this article. Jane Doe told investigators that she did not specifically remember Kretzschmar’s directly taking part in her abuse. He was not expelled from Cornell and he graduated last year, but he faced several sanctions — including writing a “reflection paper” — at the conclusion of the Title IX process and was found responsible for attempted sexual exploitation. Asked for comment on Kretzschmar’s state litigation, Giuffra simply called it “ridiculous.” On Thursday, Giuffra also revealed that Jane Doe completed a rape kit collection weeks after the incident. Kretzschmar’s attorney, Jeremy Saland, stressed to NBC News on Thursday that his client was not involved in any criminal conduct alleged in the case. “Rape allegations must be taken seriously, and the young woman at the center of this case is entitled to be heard. Nothing in our response is meant to diminish that or her,” Saland said in a statement. “However, Scott is not accused of rape and never has been. If Scott had seen Doe in duress, he would have taken action but he was not present when her alleged victimization occurred.” Saland added that his client “participated in a group chat whose content was ugly and reprehensible, and he regrets it.” The crude comments are “not the same as taking part in a rape,” and drug use allegations against Kretzschmar are also false, he said. Last month, Jane Doe sued the university, Kretzschmar and six other current or former students, alleging that what began as a consensual encounter escalated into hours of nonconsensual sexual activity. She alleges that even after she reported the incident and endured the Title IX investigation, the school and other institutions failed to do enough to protect her. (Title IX is a federal civil rights law that prohibits gender-based discrimination in educational settings that involve federal funding. As a result, U.S. colleges and universities are required to have internal processes for adjudicating claims of Title IX violations brought by their students.) The Title IX process is usually not public, but records from the investigation were made public through Kretzschmar’s Article 78 proceeding, a lawsuit he initiated in state court after he exhausted his options at Cornell. Lawyers for two of the accused men have denied wrongdoing, while the others have yet to release statements to NBC News. The Chi Phi chapter was barred from campus as a result of the allegations. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten defended his decision not to charge anyone this week, saying Jane Doe’s statement “described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual.” Kretzschmar’s Article 78 proceeding, text messages and Jane Doe’s own statements show a more complicated reality. Doe, then 20, alleges in a six-page statement to Cornell police that she arrived at Chi Phi after drinking heavily and initially entered an upstairs bedroom with two men she considered friends before things escalated. She told police she consumed ketamine for the first time that night and became increasingly impaired, drifting in and out of awareness as fraternity members filtered in and out of the room. “You look like an operating human being. [...Y]ou don’t look dead or asleep necessarily. So lights are on, but nobody’s home. Your brain is not functioning at its proper level,” Doe said at a Title IX hearing in May, detailed in Kretzschmar’s court case. Kretzschmar, however, described a far different scene when he briefly entered the room, saying in interviews with Title IX investigators that he saw nothing to suggest Jane Doe was incapacitated or in distress. He “consistently stated in his interviews, documentary submissions, and at the hearing that he did not observe [Jane Doe] naked at any time nor partake in any drug use while in the alumni room” that night, according to the Title IX panel’s report. Admitting that he had seen the initial Snapchat message before he went in the room, he told investigators that he went in briefly because he was looking for a vape and did not know whether the message “was a joke or what was going on in the [alumni] room,” according to the report. Cornell officials, in deciding to sanction Kretzschmar, noted in one filing that he“admitted he talked to someone about what was happening in the room and understood the person to say sexual activity was going on.” Kretzschmar testified that he went into the room in part to “go down and check” because he heard from one of his brothers that the “free p----y” text was real and he wanted to see what was happening. He said he was also concerned about what may have been happening because of the odd announcement. Still, he replied in the chat around 2:30 a.m. Oct. 20, 2024, that his brother’s boast about a girl in the alumni room was “not a bit.” He told investigators at a May 2025 hearing that he was “following along with what everyone else was saying” and that it was “immature and dumb.” “I shouldn’t have said it. And it is immature and a stupid text message for sure,” he said at the hearing, according to his court filings. Doe, however, told campus police her experience was far more daunting. She told police she realized at some point that she had taken ketamine earlier and then did so again because she thought that “if I do Ketamine again maybe I will pass out. My thought was that if I passed out and these men had sex with me, then they could be charged with Rape.” The next morning, after one of the defendants dropped her home and she slept for a few hours, she learned that her night had become campus gossip, according to the six-page statement she gave to campus police. In the days after her assault, Jane Doe continued to text at least one of the men, initially expressing distress over the way the encounter was being discussed on campus, according to messages NBC News obtained separately. The Chi Phi member responded with reassurances and a spin on the situation, including around Nov. 7, when Jane Doe began to doubt that he and his fraternity friends were not the source of the gossip. “I understand the regret, but personally I don’t think you have anything to be ashamed of,” the Chi Phi member told her. “The only shameful thing is how this spread and how people won’t shut up about it-which just reflects poorly on them tbh.” Jane Doe told the brother that she agreed “it’ll get better” and that “everyone needs to grow up cause sexuality and sex and s--t is changing and stuff like this is going to become more common.” Jane Doe’s attorney previously told NBC News that his client’s messages with the accused men show that she was “traumatized after the assaults and was trying to process what had occurred and get information about what happened to her and who was involved.” “She was numb and in shock at the time,” he added. “She was struggling to accept that somebody that she believed was her friend would violate and dehumanize her. It is common that survivors initially cannot accept what happened to them.” The texts also seem to show Jane Doe’s demeanor shift as she realizes something was wrong. In one message, she tells the fraternity member: “yall aren’t my friends. yall are covering your asses.” Days later, the fraternity member asks Jane Doe whether she had anything to do with his “being labeled as an assaulter in the public eye,” which she denies, saying, “i do know people are changing the narrative because like in any sexual scenario w one woman and many men the woman was probably victim” and “i know there are rumors i was gang banged.” The next day, Nov. 8, Jane Doe reported her allegations to campus police, saying in a final message to the man: “i think i’m done talking to you. i know you lied.” Kretzschmar’s own testimony in the Title IX investigation showed that, even as he denied having participated in the incident, he later questioned whether he should have recognized that something might be wrong. “I was sorry that maybe if it wasn’t consensual and she was victimized, I was sorry for not stopping it,” Kretzschmar said at a Title IX hearing in May. “And that I’m sorry I couldn’t tell if she was under the influence… just sorry that I felt like if something actually bad happened, I didn’t stop it.” Ultimately, however, the Title IX investigative panel found that Kretzschmar understood that the Snapchat message he sent “indicated some kind of sexual situation involving a female” when he chose to enter the room and that the record supported its finding that he was responsible for attempted sexual exploitation. The panel, however, did not find sufficient evidence that Kretzschmar took ketamine after it reviewed a November 2024 follicle drug test he provided independently. His punishments were focused on learning from the experience, according to documents filed in his subsequent lawsuit. Kretzschmar had to write a reflection paper on “the specific circumstances for which he was found responsible,” along with “a detailed proposal for future University educational materials to train undergraduate students around the intersection of social media use and sexual harassment, as well as bystander intervention.” He was ordered not to speak to Jane Doe for the duration of his time at Cornell and required to participate in a study at the Office of Civil Rights related to social media use, sexual harassment and bystander intervention. He was also required to help create educational programming for others about those issues. Kretzschmar and his lawyers, however, argued in state court in Tompkins County that the process was fundamentally unfair, including because he was found responsible for an offense that was not listed in his initial set of administrative charges. Among the arguments was that one of the panel members was in her car and driving during live testimony and distracted by other unrelated tasks throughout the testimony. The judge who considered the challenge found it did not matter because the underlying theory was the same. In criminal court, state Supreme Court Justice Mark Masler wrote, lesser included charges are common. “If a criminal defendant, whose liberty interests are at stake, maybe convicted of a lesser included offense with which he or she was not specifically indicted — including an attempt to commit the greater count — then the finding that petitioner was responsible for Attempted Sexual Exploitation cannot be considered to have been arbitrary and capricious,” Masler found. If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse, & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at rainn.org/get-help.

articles.title: Israeli drone kills Palestinian in Gaza, settlers kill another in West Bank
articles.summary: 1,439 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza and 5,052 injured since the ‘ceasefire’ began in October 2025.
articles.body:
An Israeli drone strike has killed a Palestinian man and wounded several others in southern Gaza while settlers shot dead another Palestinian man near Ramallah in the occupied West Bank.

The body of Tamer al-Hamayda, 42, and three wounded people were brought to Nasser Medical Complex on Thursday after the strike hit a tent sheltering displaced Palestinians in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis on the southern coast of the Gaza Strip.

Another Palestinian succumbed to wounds sustained in an earlier Israeli drone strike on Tuesday that targeted a gathering of Palestinians in Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza, according to medical personnel in Nasser Medical Complex.

Israeli forces also carried out a large-scale demolition operation targeting buildings east of Gaza City’s al-Tuffah neighbourhood.

The Gaza Health Ministry reported eight new deaths and 26 wounded over the past 24 hours, putting the toll since the “ceasefire” took effect in October 2025 at 1,439 killed and 5,052 wounded, with 834 bodies recovered from the rubble .

Israel’s war on Gaza has killed at least 74,040 Palestinians and wounded 175,168 since October 2023, the ministry said.

In the occupied West Bank, Israeli settlers shot dead a Palestinian man and wounded another during a raid on the village of Yasuf, north of Ramallah, on Thursday.

51-year-old Mashhour Yassin was shot dead by settler gunfire, the Palestinian Health Ministry said.

Describing the attack, the Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Israeli forces had detained an ambulance, seizing its key and throwing it aside, “in a crime that reflects clear coordination between the settlers and occupation forces.”

It said the killing “falls within the framework of a serious and continuous escalation in organised settler crimes,” saying Israel gives free rein to settler “terrorism against our people in the service of settlement, annexation, forced displacement and ethnic cleansing plans.”

Yasuf Mayor Jumaa Abdel Fattah told the AFP news agency that dozens of Israeli settlers armed with sticks and firearms had attacked the village, which lies between four Israeli settlements.

“Yassin was at his doorstep when the settlers attacked the village homes. He went out to defend his house,” Abdel Fattah said, adding that Yassin’s nephew was also wounded in the attack.

Abdel Fattah said the settlers had come from Havat Anton, an illegal Israeli settlement established in July that has previously attacked the village’s residents.

Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have reported a surge in settler pogrom attacks in recent months.

More than 500,000 Israelis live in West Bank settlements considered illegal under international law.

According to the UN, at least 1,112 Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the territory since October 2023, including at least 37 killed by settlers.

articles.title: Morte de estudante em Taubaté: vídeo mostra carros antes de briga | G1
articles.standfirst: Imagens mostram os veículos seguindo lado a lado momentos antes dos disparos que mataram Bruno Hashimura San Juliano, de 23 anos. Bombeiro foi preso e conseguiu liberdade provisória em audiência de custódia.
articles.summary: Morte de estudante de medicina em Taubaté: vídeo registra briga no trânsito antes dos disparos e bombeiro envolvido obteve liberdade provisória.
articles.body:
Imagens de uma câmera de segurança mostram os carros do estudante Bruno Hashimura San Juliano, de 23 anos, e do bombeiro Marcos Paulo Fujarra de Oliveira momentos antes de uma briga de trânsito que terminou com a morte do jovem, em Taubaté , no interior de SP.

O vídeo foi gravado às 6h59 desta quarta-feira (30), na Avenida do Povo. Nas imagens, os dois veículos aparecem seguindo pela via. Bruno está um pouco à frente, à esquerda da imagem.

Conforme os carros avançam, eles ficam lado a lado. Em um trecho da gravação, em câmera lenta, é possível ver o bombeiro fazendo gestos.

Os dois veículos continuam lado a lado até um semáforo. Quando os carros param, a luz de freio do veículo conduzido pelo bombeiro se apaga e ele desce.

Uma placa de trânsito encobre parte da cena e impede que a câmera registre o que aconteceu naquele momento. Na sequência, Bruno sai pela porta do passageiro e corre. Ele foi atingido por quatro disparos e morreu.

Imagens mostram carros de estudante e bombeiro antes de briga de trânsito que terminou em morte em Taubaté. — Foto: Reprodução

Uma guia de encaminhamento médico registra que Bruno sofreu quatro ferimentos provocados por arma de fogo: um no pescoço, dois no tórax e um no braço esquerdo.

Estudante de Medicina Bruno Hashimura San Juliano, de 23 anos, morreu após ser baleado durante uma discussão de trânsito em Taubaté. — Foto: Arte g1

Marcos Paulo foi preso em flagrante ainda na quarta-feira. Segundo a polícia, ele afirmou estar arrependido e disse que não premeditou os disparos. O bombeiro está licenciado do cargo desde maio e a corporação lamentou o caso.

Nesta quinta-feira (1º), durante audiência de custódia, a juíza Gláucia Paiva concedeu liberdade provisória ao bombeiro.

Na decisão, a magistrada considerou que Marcos Paulo é primário e que não havia circunstâncias suficientes para indicar que a liberdade dele representaria risco à ordem pública. Ele terá que cumprir medidas cautelares, entre elas não sair de casa durante a noite.

Nesta quinta-feira à tarde, o Ministério Público de São Paulo recorreu da decisão que concedeu liberdade provisória a Marcos Paulo Fujarra de Oliveira e pediu a decretação da prisão preventiva dele.

A dinâmica do que aconteceu quando os dois carros pararam no semáforo ainda é investigada. A defesa do bombeiro afirma que ele agiu em legítima defesa após ser ameaçado com um objeto que parecia ser uma arma.

"A polícia judiciária ainda está em diligências por testemunhas, por câmeras do trajeto dos locais dos fatos, pra poder elucidar aí também a nossa tese de legítima defesa", afirmou o advogado Claudio Rodrigues Moreira.

Uma testemunha ouvida pela polícia apresentou uma versão diferente. Segundo o depoimento, o bombeiro teria ido até o carro de Bruno, quebrado o vidro e efetuado os disparos, sem que houvesse uma ameaça. A família de Bruno contesta a versão apresentada pela defesa.

"Ele tava voltando da faculdade, ele estudava... era isso. Família que amava ele. Vai trazer de volta? Não vai. Ele não matou meu primo, ele matou a família inteira", disse Felipe San Juliano, primo de Bruno.

A investigação deve analisar imagens de câmeras de segurança e ouvir testemunhas para esclarecer a dinâmica da ocorrência.

articles.summary: Programação também conta com stand up com Renato Albani, Life Expo Wellness e peças teatrais. Veja o que fazer no Distrito Federal entre sexta-feira (2) e domingo (4).
articles.body:
Alcione (ao centro), Jorge Aragão (á esquerda) e Zeca Pagodinho se juntam na turnê 'O maior encontro do samba' — Foto: Divulgação

O primeiro fim de semana do mês de outubro chegou com diferentes tipos de atrações no Distrito Federal. Um destaque é "O Maior Encontro do Samba", com Zeca Pagodinho, Alcione e Jorge Aragão, que acontece neste sábado (3), no Na Praia Parque.

Também no sábado, a banda Jovem Dionísio se apresenta na Infinu. E para os fãs de stand up comedy, Renato Albani apresenta seu novo espetáculo "Salve-se Quem Puder", no Centro de Convenções Ulysses Guimarães.

A programação também conta com Buraco do Jazz, Life Expo Wellness e peças teatrais. Veja o que fazer no Distrito Federal entre sexta-feira (2) e domingo (4):

Zeca Pagodinho, Alcione e Jorge Aragão em 'O Maior Encontro do Samba'

Jovem Dionísio traz turnê do disco Migalhas para a Infinu

Renato Albani apresenta novo espetáculo 'Salve-se Quem Puder'

Buraco do Jazz encerra temporada de 10 anos neste mês de outubro

Projeto Celebrando Rita Lee no Eye Patch Panda

'A Monstrinha Corajosa' no Teatro Brasília Shopping

Gole de Poesia reúne literatura periférica, música e hip-hop no Mercado Sul em Taguatinga

Zeca Pagodinho, Alcione e Jorge Aragão chegam a Brasília, neste sábado (3), para uma noite dedicada a um repertório que ajuda a contar a história da música brasileira. "O Maior Encontro do Samba" foi concebido a partir da ideia de que o gênero se fortalece quando histórias e referências compartilham o mesmo espaço.

Entre os destaques do repertório estão "Eu e Você Sempre', "A Loba", "Sufoco", "Não Sou Mais Disso" e "Lama nas Ruas". A combinação de clássicos, timbres e interação entre os artistas cria uma dinâmica que permeia a emoção e a celebração.

📍 Local: Na Praia Parque - Setor de Clubes Esportivos Sul, Trecho 2, Asa Sul – Brasília/DF

🎫 Ingressos: a partir de R$ 177,50, pelo site

Jovem Dionísio traz turnê do disco 'Migalhas' para a Infinu

O grupo paranaense Jovem Dionísio lança o terceiro álbum, 'Migalhas', em 1º de abril — Foto: Fernando Mendes / Divulgação

A banda Jovem Dionísio, de Curitiba, traz o novo show para a Infinu em Brasília, neste sábado (3). A apresentação faz parte da turnê do disco mais recente, "Migalhas", lançado em abril de 2026.

Conhecidos por músicas animadas que misturam rock, indie, alternativo, pop e uma pitada de hip-hop, a banda se afasta um pouco da sonoridade dos hits "Acorda Pedrinho", "Tô bem" e "Ponto de Exclamação" e propõe uma performance mais imersiva e sóbria nos novos shows que tem feito. Migalhas é um álbum gravado inteiramente ao vivo e a apresentação é um convite para o público entrar em uma ambiente de estúdio com a Jovem Dionísio.

📍 Local: Infinu Comunidade Criativa (SQS 506 – Brasília/DF)

🎫 Ingressos: a partir de R$ 60, pelo site

Renato Albani chega pela primeira vez a Brasília com seu novo espetáculo, "Salve-se Quem Puder". A apresentação acontece neste sábado (3), no Centro de Convenções Ulysses Guimarães.

No espetáculo, Albani parte de memórias de uma infância imperfeita, mas vivida com mais leveza, para estabelecer um contraponto com a exaustão dos dias atuais. Entre situações cotidianas, observações bem-humoradas e histórias pessoais, o comediante aborda cobranças, expectativas, relacionamentos e as preocupações que fazem parte da vida moderna.

📍 Local: Centro de Convenções Ulysses Guimarães

Com a chegada da primavera e o prenúncio das chuvas, o Buraco do Jazz prepara a sua despedida com aquela combinação de música, natureza e gente reunida. Os encontros estão confirmados semanalmente às quintas e sextas-feiras, no Centro Cultural Três Poderes.

O primeiro fim de semana desta despedida traz Serpa Blues Band, nesta sexta-feira (2).

🎫 Entrada gratuita, com contribuição voluntária

A Life Expo Wellness continua em Brasília. Após o sucesso da segunda edição, o evento anuncia o Extra Weekend do Life Expo, com dois dias adicionais de programação no Parque da Cidade, nesta sexta-feira (2) e sábado (3).

Serão mais dois dias com todas as atividades que o público pôde aproveitar no primeiro fim de semana, como a Arena Cycling, dedicada ao ciclismo indoor, aulas de Kangoo Jump, funcional fight, meditação, yoga, mobilidade, futmesa, altinha, HYROX e Área Recovery com massagem, sauna, limpeza de pele e banheira de gelo.

Na sexta-feira, a programação acontece das 16h às 21h. Já no sábado, o evento retorna das 8h às 18h, mantendo a entrada gratuita e o Estacionamento 11 do Parque da Cidade como ponto de encontro.

Com cerimonial da atriz Marília Abreu, o 4º Romaria Poética traz apresentações de Margô Oliveira, Cumpadi Ancelmo, Davi Mello, Yure Pierre, Seu Mané Loko Guará, Gilson Alencar & Convidados, Cantos Sazonais, Luizão do Forró, Mamulengo Fuzuê e Tambor de Crioula Flores de São Benedito. Músicas como "Top Top", "Agora Só Falta Você" e "Mania de Você" dão o tom do que a Celebrando Rita Lee prepara para essa apresentação intimista. A banda, formada por Michele Chitko (voz), Paulo Veríssimo (guitarra/voz), Renato Azambuja (percussão/voz), Ivo Portela (baixo/voz), Marcos Henrique (teclado) e Maicon Vasconcelos (bateria), promete uma noite de muito rock’n’roll, energia e celebração da obra de uma das maiores referências do rock brasileiro.

articles.title: O que o caso de Christa Pike diz sobre a pena de morte nos EUA | G1
articles.standfirst: A falha na execução da prisioneira condenada à morte Christa Pike no Tennessee volta a chamar a atenção para a pena de morte e sua forma de aplicação nos Estados Unidos.
articles.summary: A falha na execução da prisioneira condenada à morte Christa Pike no Tennessee volta a chamar a atenção para a pena de morte e sua forma de aplicação nos Estados Unidos.
articles.body:
A americana Christa Pike, condenada à morte no Estado americano do Tennessee, foi levada ao hospital após uma tentativa frustrada de execução por injeção letal, segundo seus advogados.

Um dos advogados declarou à BBC que Pike, de 50 anos, está agora sob tratamento médico no hospital, após a administração de duas seringas de pentobarbital.

Os detalhes sobre os motivos que levaram a execução a ser mal sucedida ainda estão sendo revelados.

Pike foi condenada à morte em 1996, pelo assassinato de Colleen Slemmer, de 19 anos. Sua execução foi objeto de uma batalha legal no último minuto.

Esta foi a segunda execução fracassada no Tennessee em 2026. Em maio, autoridades postergaram a injeção letal de Tony Carruthers, condenado pelo sequestro e assassinato de três pessoas em 1994.

Os funcionários encarregados não conseguiram encontrar uma veia para administrar a droga letal.

A execução de Christa Pike foi objeto de uma batalha judicial no último minuto — Foto: Reuters/Getty Images/BBC

Em 1976, a Suprema Corte americana suspendeu sua proibição temporária da pena de morte.

Desde então, 1.683 pessoas foram executadas nos Estados Unidos , segundo o Centro de Informações sobre a Pena de Morte (DPIC, na sigla em inglês). Destas, 18 eram mulheres, o que representa cerca de 1% das execuções.

O banco de dados da organização mostra que 47 pessoas foram executadas em 2025 — o número mais alto desde 2009. Foi um aumento sensível em relação aos 25 casos de 2024.

Mas o apoio popular à pena de morte encontra-se no seu nível mais baixo dos últimos 50 anos.

Uma recente pesquisa do instituto Gallup concluiu que 52% dos americanos apoiavam a prática em 2025. Segundo a mesma pesquisa, 44% se opunham à pena capital, o que representa o maior índice de oposição registrado pelo Gallup desde maio de 1966.

Desde 1976, os Estados americanos utilizam cinco métodos principais de execução:

A injeção letal ainda é, de longe, o método de execução mais comum. Ele representa 89% do total das execuções desde 1976.

Segundo o DPIC, todos os Estados que realizam execuções atualmente utilizam este método, embora vários deles também autorizem formas alternativas.

A forca não é usada em nenhum Estado desde 1996, quando Delaware executou Billy Bailey.

New Hampshire havia mantido o método como alternativa, caso a injeção letal fosse impraticável. Mas o Estado aboliu a pena de morte em 2019.

A medida não foi retroativa, de forma que ainda existe um prisioneiro que permanece no corredor da morte. New Hampshire não executa nenhum prisioneiro desde 1939.

A pena capital permanece legal em 27 Estados americanos, bem como sob as leis federais e militares.

Quatro Estados suspenderam as execuções (Califórnia, Ohio, Oregon e Pensilvânia) e vários outros, onde a pena de morte é legal, não realizam execuções há anos.

Já a Flórida foi responsável por 19 execuções em 2025, o que representa cerca de 40% do total nacional.

A injeção letal ainda é, de longe, o método mais comum de execução, aplicado em cerca de 89% dos casos — Foto: Getty Images via BBC

Historicamente, muitos Estados utilizavam um protocolo de três drogas:

Anestésico ou sedativo (frequentemente, tiopental sódico, depois midazolam)

Agente paralisante (brometo de vecurônio)

Cloreto de potássio para fazer o coração parar

Tiopental sódico foi amplamente empregado em injeções letais por anos. Mas as companhias farmacêuticas passaram a se opor cada vez mais ao uso dos seus medicamentos nas execuções.

Os fabricantes suspenderam o fornecimento de drogas para este propósito e as restrições de exportação europeias reduziram ainda mais a sua disponibilidade.

Muitos Estados passaram a adotar um protocolo de uma única droga, pentobarbital. Uma grande dose do barbiturato é administrada ao prisioneiro para reduzir sua atividade cerebral e a respiração.

Na época, a droga era amplamente disponível nos Estados Unidos. Em doses menores, ela é empregada como sedativo e no controle de convulsões. Seu uso também é comum na medicina veterinária, para realizar eutanásia em animais.

O governo federal americano usou a substância como sua única droga de execução desde a adoção do protocolo de uma única droga em 2019, apesar da sua baixa disponibilidade.

Como resultado, muitos Estados procuraram as farmácias de manipulação, que produzem lotes sob encomenda e sofrem menos regulamentação que os fabricantes de medicamentos.

Diversos Estados também aprovaram leis para proteger a identidade dos fornecedores. Por isso, muitas vezes não se sabe ao certo de onde vieram as drogas.

Ainda assim, um memorando de 48 páginas do Departamento de Justiça dos Estados Unidos, publicado em abril, chama a substância de "padrão-ouro das drogas de injeção letal".

O DPIC afirma que a dificuldade cada vez maior de obtenção legal das drogas empregadas em execuções levou alguns Estados a experimentar novas drogas e combinações.

Este procedimento resultou em execuções prolongadas, com prisioneiros exibindo sinais de dor e estresse. Além disso, a escassez da droga também elevou os custos das execuções.

Em 2014, o governador de Oklahoma suspendeu as execuções no Estado, após uma injeção letal mal sucedida.

A Louisiana também deixou de realizar execuções por 15 anos, devido a falhas na aquisição das drogas. O intervalo terminou em 18 de março de 2025, com a execução de Jessie Hoffman Jr., usando gás nitrogênio.

Quem é Christa Pike — Foto: Tennesse Department of Corrections/BBC

O memorando do Departamento de Justiça também orientou as prisões federais a expandir o leque de métodos de execução e incluir fuzilamento, asfixia com gás e eletrocução.

O órgão declarou que a mudança "fortaleceria" a pena de morte, por "dissuadir os crimes mais bárbaros, oferecer justiça para as vítimas e fornecer a conclusão devida há muito tempo para os entes queridos sobreviventes".

O governo do ex-presidente Joe Biden (2021-2025) decretou moratória da maior parte das execuções federais. E, antes de deixar o poder, Biden perdoou 37 dos 40 prisioneiros federais no corredor da morte.

Já o atual presidente, Donald Trump, apoia há muito tempo a pena de morte. Ele orientou o Departamento de Justiça a retomar as execuções no primeiro dia do seu segundo mandato, em janeiro do ano passado.

A eletrocução já foi um dos principais métodos de execução, mas sua aplicação, agora, é rara.

Atualmente, nove Estados americanos autorizam o uso da cadeira elétrica. A Carolina do Sul fez da eletrocução seu método padrão, enquanto os outros oito Estados a mantém como opção ou backup, com a injeção letal como padrão.

Desde 1976, 163 execuções foram realizadas por eletrocução, mas apenas 19 desde 2000. A última ocorreu no Tennessee, em 2020.

O fuzilamento já foi considerado uma relíquia do passado.

Mas a Carolina do Sul retomou as execuções por fuzilamento em 2025. Idaho fez do fuzilamento seu principal método de execução em julho de 2026, depois das dificuldades para obter drogas de injeção letal.

O Alabama se tornou o primeiro Estado a executar um prisioneiro por hipóxia por nitrogênio em 2024. A Louisiana veio em seguida, em março de 2025.

O método consiste em privar o prisioneiro de oxigênio, forçando-o a respirar nitrogênio puro.

Seus defensores o descrevem como uma alternativa prática à injeção letal, mas outros alegam que o método passou por poucos testes e levanta sérias preocupações éticas.

Sala de execução na Prisão Estadual de San Quentin, na Califórnia, Estados Unidos. — Foto: California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation

Os críticos da pena de morte defendem que as dificuldades para a obtenção de drogas para injeção letal, aliadas a uma série de execuções problemáticas, trouxeram questionamentos se as execuções podem ser realizadas de forma humana.

Os questionamentos legais, muitas vezes, se concentraram nas preocupações de que alguns protocolos de drogas podem causar dores ou sofrimento desnecessário. Ativistas afirmam que eles violam a Constituição americana, que proíbe punições cruéis e incomuns.

Seus oponentes também indicam a falta de transparência, já que a identidade dos fornecedores é protegida em alguns Estados. Esta medida dificulta a investigação da fonte e da qualidade das drogas empregadas nas execuções.

Alguns críticos também defendem que o impacto das execuções se estende para além dos prisioneiros e das famílias das vítimas.

Em entrevista à BBC em 2014, o diretor do sistema prisional do Estado americano da Geórgia nos anos 1990, Allen Ault, descreveu o impacto psicológico permanente das execuções para as autoridades e diretores de presídios, além das equipes médicas e das testemunhas.

"Ainda tenho pesadelos", contou Ault à BBC. "É a forma mais premeditada de assassinato que você pode imaginar e ela permanece na sua psique para sempre."

articles.title: Gavin Newsom signs Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha into law as new California state holidays
articles.summary: Gov. Gavin Newsom signed the Muslim days Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha into law as California state holidays before signing bills protecting Jewish holidays.
articles.body: California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed into law a bill that formally recognizes two Muslim holidays as state holidays on Sunday, making it the second state to formally recognize both holidays statewide. California Assembly Bill 2017 officially added Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha to the list of state holidays, which would permit public schools and colleges to close and allow state employees to be eligible to observe the holidays. However, schools and businesses will not be required to close on these days, and courts will be required to stay open. This makes California the second state in the country, after Washington state, to pass statewide legislation recognizing the Muslim holidays. DEI HIRING BOOST FOR ONE BLUE STATE'S MUSLIM COMMISSION INITIATIVE FLIES IN FACE OF TRUMP'S ANTI-WOKE PUSH Before signing AB 2017, Newsom had multiple bills on his desk that provided protections and exceptions for other religious observances, including Jewish holidays such as Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. For example, AB 395, which reached the governor days before AB 2017, would codify these Jewish holidays, among others, into state law and require state agencies and facilities like schools to "make every reasonable effort" to avoid scheduling significant functions for those days. Another bill, AB 1763, would also guarantee students in K-12 be allowed excused absences for religious holidays. Though these bills were introduced and presented to the governor before AB 2017, Newsom did not sign the additional bills into law until Wednesday, prior to the midnight deadline. Republican opponents criticized Newsom for appearing to prioritize bills recognizing Muslim holidays over bills allowing for equal treatment for Jewish holidays. SWING STATE MAYOR SUED AS CITY’S MUSLIM HOLIDAY DISPLAYS IGNITE RELIGIOUS-FAVORITISM FIGHT "The fact that Newsom chose to sign the Eid law before the law that protected other religious observance speaks volumes about the direction he is moving as he eyes a 2028 run for the presidency," Elizabeth Barcohana, chair of Jewish engagement for the California Republican Party, told Cleveland Jewish News (JNS) Thursday. She also warned that these laws would give Muslim holidays additional privileges not afforded to other religions, which could include closing schools. "People may think this is alarmist, but this is an example of American laws adopting a Sharia law framework," Barcohana told JNS. "Special protections no other religious observance receives, the option to shut down public institutions to observe the holiday that, until now, only Christian holidays received and curriculum in public schools that is religious in nature notably about a religion that emphasizes conversion." However, David Bocarsly, CEO of Jewish California, supported Newsom's actions, saying he was not concerned about the order in which the bills were signed because all three became law. CALIFORNIA LAWMAKERS' PUSH TO MAKE MUSLIM HOLY DAYS STATE HOLIDAYS SPARKS DEBATE OVER SCHOOL NEUTRALITY "With more than 1,000 bills in front of him this past month, we aren't concerned with the sequencing of Assembly Bill 395 and Assembly Bill 1763, as long as they got signed, and they did. We're thrilled to see these two critical religious freedom protections become law and to recognize three Jewish holidays in California statute for the first time," Bocarsly told Fox News Digital. His organization also celebrated Newsom signing into law SB 1387, which recognizes Jewish identity as an ethnicity. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment but did not immediately receive a response. A spokesperson for Newsom's office told Fox News Digital, "This is not about manufacturing a scorecard among faiths. The Governor signs bills based on the substance of the legislation and the constitutional process governing when he receives and acts on bills. California is proud to continue strengthening its religious freedom – something our nation’s founders strongly believed in, too."

articles.title: Major airport suffers fourth near miss in recent months as jet is forced to brake hard
articles.summary: Transport safety officials revealed staffing levels and fatigue at Sydney Airport's control tower as key areas of inquiry after recent runway incursions in three months.
articles.body: A major international airport is facing mounting scrutiny after investigators released preliminary findings into a series of runway incidents and near collisions. The incidents, which involved passenger aircraft, all occurred at Sydney Airport during the past three months. The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) released preliminary reports Sept. 30. STAGGERING DRUG HAUL FOUND AT MAJOR AIRPORT AFTER BIZARRE ATTEMPT TO HIDE EVIDENCE The incidents began July 27, when a Qantas Boeing 737 was cleared to cross a runway in front of a QantasLink Dash 8 that was landing, according to the ATSB. On Aug. 9, a Jetstar Airbus A320 was forced to brake abruptly to avoid a Qatar Airways Boeing 777 being towed across its path. A flight attendant aboard the Jetstar aircraft fell during that sudden braking and fractured her wrist. The same day, a Qantas Boeing 737 was cleared to cross a runway in front of a Virgin Australia 737 that had just been cleared for takeoff, the report said. Nine days later, a Qantas Airbus A321 had to brake while taxiing to allow another Qantas 737 to pass in front of it. SKYDIVERS WATCH PLANE VANISH FROM SIGHT, MAKE SPLIT-SECOND DECISION TO JUMP In a statement to Fox News Digital Thursday, Sydney Airport said safety was its "highest priority." "We will continue to support the Minister and Airservices as they work through the preliminary findings and the appropriate actions," a spokesperson said. "We await the final reports and any recommendations arising from the ATSB’s investigations." Staffing levels at Sydney Airport's control tower had emerged as a recurring area of inquiry, investigators said, although they have not determined whether staffing factors directly contributed to any of the recent incidents. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "These investigations will look to understand the significance of staff resourcing pressures within the tower, specifically, the practice of combining operational roles, the routine reliance on overtime to fill shifts and training or supervision activities being conducted alongside operational duties," Angus Mitchell, ATSB chief commissioner, said in a press release. Investigators also raised concerns about fatigue, though they cautioned that a heightened risk of fatigue does not necessarily mean controllers were tired at the time of the incidents. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "We are examining the effectiveness of the measures in place to manage this identified risk," Mitchell added. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The incidents came as Sydney Airport recorded the highest rate of ground conflicts per aircraft movement among Australia's major airports in the post-COVID period, about 20% above the national average, according to a separate ATSB analysis. Mitchell cautioned that the findings should "be viewed in the context of Sydney Airport being the most complex in the country." articles.title: US energy department engineer held for alleged Houthi links, drone and explosives support
articles.summary: A US department of energy electrical engineer has been arrested for allegedly providing material support to the Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
articles.body: A US department of energy electrical engineer has been arrested for allegedly providing material support to the Iran-backed Houthi rebels. He allegedly bought materials for homemade explosives and drone parts and travelled to Yemen, the US justice department said Thursday.Ashton Hamed Ellaboudy, 51, of Richland, Washington, was arrested Thursday and is expected to appear in court for the first time on Friday. He faces charges under a US law that prohibits providing material support to organisations designated as foreign terrorist organisations. The Houthis are designated as such by the US.Alleged Yemen tripAccording to an FBI affidavit, Ellaboudy travelled to Yemen in September last year with the stated aim of helping the Houthis improve their communications capabilities. Investigators said he told FBI informants that he had to be smuggled into and out of Yemen.Ellaboudy allegedly hoped to reach Sanaa, the Houthi-controlled capital, to establish government-level contacts. The FBI said he was ultimately unable to reach the capital.After returning to the US, Ellaboudy allegedly told Customs and Border Protection officers that he had travelled from Oman on a work trip and was part of a US government mission to inspect defence facilities.His supervisor, however, told investigators that he had no knowledge of Ellaboudy's international travel or any Energy Department missile inspection programme involving him, according to the affidavit.Explosive materials, drone partsThe FBI began investigating Ellaboudy after learning that he had bought precursor chemicals that can be used to make homemade explosives. These included acetone and sodium bisulphate.Investigators also found that he had purchased components used for drones, the FBI said.During the investigation, Ellaboudy communicated with several informants. One of them was posing as a Houthi colonel. Authorities allege that Ellaboudy provided advice and assistance on communications equipment as part of his efforts to help the group.Houthi conflictThe allegations come as Yemen has again seen violence between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces. The conflict began in 2014 when the Iran-backed rebels seized Sanaa, forcing Yemen's government into exile in Saudi Arabia.The renewed fighting has killed hundreds of people and displaced tens of thousands, according to the information cited by the Justice Department.“These allegations are so deeply disturbing that they almost defy imagination,” John Eisenberg, an assistant attorney general in charge of the Justice Department's National Security Division, said in a statement.Court records did not list an attorney available to speak on Ellaboudy's behalf.You use AI every day. articles.title: UK-Mauritius Chagos sovereignty deal stalls amid fears of further delays
articles.summary: Renewed talks over the stalled agreement have revived hope of resettlement, but ageing Chagossians fear time is running.
articles.body:
Pointe aux Sables, Mauritius – “At one funeral, we scattered sand from Chagos into an elder’s tomb to honour his unfulfilled wish to breathe his last in his homeland,” says Olivier Bancoult of the Chagos Refugees Group.

For elderly Chagossians displaced from their Indian Ocean homeland decades ago, delays to a treaty allowing their return are raising fears that they may never see the islands again.

The agreement, signed by Britain and Mauritius in May 2025, would allow resettlement on islands other than Diego Garcia, which would remain a military base. But it has yet to enter into force amid opposition from US President Donald Trump.

“We remain unshaken by Trump’s interference in the Chagos deal,” Bancoult says.

“The 2019 ICJ advisory opinion in favour of the archipelago’s return to Mauritius has restored our dignity and faith in our rights as native Chagossians.”

The Chagos archipelago, a group of islands in the Indian Ocean, was separated from Mauritius by Britain in 1965, three years before Mauritius gained independence. Britain later established a military base with the US on Diego Garcia, the largest island in the group.

Between 1968 and 1973, Britain removed an estimated 1,400 to 1,700 Chagossians from the islands. Many were resettled in Mauritius and the Seychelles, with others later moving to the United Kingdom. British authorities also made it illegal to remain on or return to the islands without permission.

“If Trump wants to meddle in this matter, well, let him,” Bancoult says. “We’ve had the 2019 ICJ [International Court of Justice] advisory opinion, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea’s 2021 judgement, and the 2025 UK-Mauritius treaty providing for Mauritius to exercise sovereignty over the archipelago. International law is squarely on our side.”

Signed on May 22, 2025, the treaty provides for Mauritius to exercise sovereignty over the Chagos archipelago, while allowing the UK to exercise rights over the Diego Garcia military base for an initial 99-year period. It also allows Mauritius to arrange for the resettlement of Chagossians on islands other than Diego Garcia. The treaty has not yet entered into force.

In April, the UK government told Parliament that the legislation needed to implement the agreement could not complete its passage during the 2024–26 parliamentary session. The session ended on April 29, meaning the bill made no further progress.

In January, Trump criticised the agreement , calling it an “act of great stupidity ” and questioning whether it adequately protected the Diego Garcia military base.

The issue returned to the diplomatic agenda in September. On September 21, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK would work with Mauritius and the US on a way forward that secures the operation of Diego Garcia and protects UK national security.

On September 26, Mauritian Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam travelled to the UK for talks with British National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell and other officials on the Chagos issue. He remains in London, with the Mauritian government saying the discussions would cover recent developments concerning the archipelago.

For Bancoult, the central question is whether elderly Chagossians will live long enough to see the treaty’s promises fulfilled.

“Chagossians born on the archipelago are now aged between 58 and 100. We are growing old, and we have lost several Chagossian elders this year alone,” he says.

For younger Chagossians, the consequences are also cultural.

Chrisyl Wong-Hang-Sun, a PhD researcher in anthropology at the University of Edinburgh, says years of displacement and migration are making it harder to preserve Chagossian culture.

“During my fieldwork, many diaspora members expressed concerns over cultural loss, such as words in Chagossian Creole and recipes that are difficult to recreate abroad,” she says. “Descendants of Chagossians, myself included, long to know the islands of their relatives and ancestors.”

The dispute has also exposed political differences among Chagossians.

“The actions of both the British and Mauritian governments have resulted in very nuanced and differing political opinions among Chagossians across the UK, Mauritius and the Seychelles,” Wong-Hang-Sun says.

The Chagos Refugees Group is at odds with UK-based second-generation Chagossian Misley Mandarin and his supporters, who favour resettlement under British rather than Mauritian sovereignty and have received backing from Reform UK.

Wong-Hang-Sun says those differences should be recognised as negotiations continue.

Both governments, she says, need to “find ways to prioritise and engage with the Chagossian diaspora as a whole”.

Mauritius has disclosed little publicly about the substance of the latest talks on Chagos.

At the United Nations General Assembly in September, Foreign Minister Dhananjay Ramful reiterated Mauritius’ position that its sovereignty over the Chagos archipelago was “non-negotiable”. He also described the 2025 agreement as a vindication of international law and said Mauritius was committed to diplomacy and dialogue over the issue.

Beyond official statements and communiques, the Mauritian government has provided few details about the substance of the current discussions.

International relations consultant Bruno Donat, who has previously worked at the UN, says Mauritius should focus on sustained engagement with diplomatic partners, including the African Union, small island states, the Commonwealth Secretariat and sympathetic voices in the US Congress.

“Being in New York corridors for a photo” is not the priority, Donat says. Sustained engagement, he argues, can build pressure on Washington and prevent the issue from remaining unresolved indefinitely.

The Chagos Refugees Group has pursued a similar approach. In June, two months after the treaty stalled, its members travelled to the UK to lobby representatives of British political parties, with the exception of Reform UK.

But Diego Garcia remains the most contentious part of the agreement.

Lalit, a Mauritian political organisation that has campaigned for decades for the closure of the base, opposes its continued military use. Lindsey Collen of Lalit says the treaty, as it stood in April, would have kept the base open and brought Mauritius into a closer relationship with the US military presence on the island.

“In addition to the moral responsibility, we have the knowledge that we might become a target for self-defence if our land is used this way,” she says.

Collen is also concerned about a new partnership between the Mauritius Police Force and the New Mexico National Guard, as well as what she describes as the “enormous military-looking buildings” of the new US embassy in Mauritius.

Donat argues that the treaty could instead give Mauritius greater leverage over how Diego Garcia is used.

“Mauritius has publicly stated that the strikes launched from Diego Garcia against Iran breached international law,” he says. “That is not the position of a government staying silent to protect a lease payment.”

For Bancoult, those wider strategic questions are secondary to the need to ensure that elderly Chagossians have the chance to return to their homeland during their lifetimes.

“We are opposed to war, ethically, but we are also running out of time.”

The Chagos Refugees Group hopes to soon celebrate the 101st birthday of one of its members.

“God willing, he’ll stay with us for more years,” Bancoult says.

articles.title: DOE employee charged with trying to aid Iran-backed Houthis, feds say
articles.summary: Ashton Hamed Ellaboudy allegedly used his electrical engineering expertise in an attempt to aid Houthi communications, drones and homemade explosives production.
articles.body: A U.S. Department of Energy worker from Richland, Washington, was arrested Thursday and charged with attempting to provide "material support" to the Iran-backed Houthis, according to the Department of Justice (DOJ). Ashton Hamed Ellaboudy, 51, is accused of attempting to use his electrical engineering knowledge and background to support the terrorist group in improving its mobile communications infrastructure, secure components for drones as well as chemicals for homemade explosives. articles.title: Rubio waives human rights restrictions to release $320 million in military aid to Egypt
articles.summary: Egypt has been a key mediator between the U.S. and Iran in the efforts to wind down the more than seven-month-long conflict.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Secretary of State Marco Rubio has waived a restriction on $320 million in military aid to Egypt that had been previously withheld over human rights concerns, citing Egypt’s help in dealing with Iran since the conflict began earlier this year. The State Department said Thursday that Rubio had signed off on the waiver “in the interest of U.S. national security.” “The Secretary’s determination reflects the importance of Egypt to U.S. national security interests, and the concrete security cooperation Egypt provides to the United States,” the department said. In a letter sent to lawmakers whose contents were shared with The Associated Press, Rubio cited, in particular, Egypt’s “helpful role” in the war with Iran. Egypt has been a key mediator between the U.S. and Iran in the efforts to wind down the more than seven-month-long conflict. The State Department maintained that the Trump administration would continue to raise human rights matters as part of its dialogue with Egypt “on the full range of issues in our bilateral relationship.” “The waiver determination recognizes the importance of maintaining security cooperation with Egypt at a time of significant regional security challenges,” the department said. The $320 million is part of an annual U.S. contribution of $1.3 billion in economic and military assistance to Egypt. Specifically, it is for foreign military financing, which provides money for recipient nations to purchase U.S.-produced weaponry. Congress inserted the requirement over concerns about Egypt’s human rights record, which many experts regard as problematic. The State Department itself in recent years has pointed to credible reports of torture, arbitrary arrest, child labor and restrictions on expression. But granting a waiver to Egypt has become routine for both Republican and Democratic administrations. The Biden administration, for example, last issued a waiver in September 2024, citing Egypt’s assistance in U.S. efforts to bring an end to the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza.

articles.title: GREGG JARRETT: My mother’s advice led me to the career of a lifetime
articles.summary: Former trial lawyer Gregg Jarrett reflects on leaving his legal career behind and finding purpose during nearly 25 years at the network's news operation.
articles.body: Decades ago, when I was agonizing over the decision to forsake my profession as a trial lawyer to pursue a far riskier and more uncertain career in television news, my mother offered sage advice. "The worst thing you can do is choose the easy course and be haunted by regret over what might have been," she said. I embraced her counsel, realizing that the only thing scarier than change is the absence of imagination. I quit my secure and lucrative job as an attorney in San Francisco and moved forward into the unknown. Fortunately, I was too naive to understand that the chances of success were remote. I discovered that change hurts. It can be difficult and discouraging. But the fear of failure forced me to persevere. My early ventures up the ladder from local news channels to larger network operations felt like Churchill’s "wilderness years." It was a long slog in search of advancement and fulfillment. Self-doubt was always hovering nearby. DANA PERINO: THE UNTOLD STORY OF THE REMARKABLE PEOPLE WHO MAKE FOX NEWS POSSIBLE But all of that vanished when I landed at Fox News nearly a quarter of a century ago. I have been grateful ever since to have played a small role in a network that has changed the face of television news for the better. I could tell at the outset that the people at Fox were different. They were dedicated and passionate. The common denominator was an unwavering commitment to excellence. We supported one another. I could tell at the outset that the people at Fox were different. They were dedicated and passionate. The common denominator was an unwavering commitment to excellence. We supported one another. But the heart and soul of our network are the viewers themselves. They watch with consistency because they trust what they see and hear. They feel engaged. In turn, those of us on air and the many people behind the scenes do our level best to maintain that trust by providing the highest-quality news and information available. As a 24-hour news operation, that level of devotion and diligence is not easy to sustain. Yet I am consistently impressed by the energy, creativity and intelligence that my colleagues bring to the on-air product every hour of every day. They are tireless and enthusiastic even when they have every right not to be. Those are rare qualities. MARTHA MACCALLUM: AFTER 22 YEARS, HERE'S WHY I'M GRATEFUL TO CALL FOX HOME During my many years at Fox, I have covered a multitude of stories — the War on Terror, hurricanes, disasters, presidential elections, the dot-com crash, financial calamities, social upheavals, cultural controversies, criminal trials, Supreme Court decisions and the COVID-19 pandemic, to name a few. Fox never said "no" when I wanted to venture beyond the newsroom. They encouraged it. I have grown and evolved in ways that I never imagined. Fox made that possible. And I’ve enjoyed every minute of it. Having previously reported from conflict zones in the Middle East, I volunteered in 2003 as a correspondent during the Iraq War. For a time, I was embedded with the 3rd Infantry Division. These were courageous young soldiers who took good care of me. The experience gave me a renewed respect and admiration for our nation’s military. There is none better anywhere. Smartphones, e-commerce, social media, cloud computing and AI have transformed our lives. The Dow Jones Industrial Average hovered around 10,000 back then. It now exceeds 50,000. In my time at Fox News, I have served as an anchor, reporter, documentary host, opinion columnist and, most recently, legal analyst for the network. I penned four books along the way. I have grown and evolved in ways that I never imagined. Fox made that possible. And I’ve enjoyed every minute of it.
