articles.title: Governor replaces DA with New York AG Letitia James as special prosecutor in Cornell case
articles.summary: Jane Doe, who has said she was raped and plied with drugs at a Cornell fraternity house in 2024, “deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued,” Gov. Kathy Hochul said.
articles.body: New York Attorney General Letitia James has been appointed as special prosecutor in the Cornell University sexual assault investigation, Gov. Kathy Hochul announced Thursday, following increasing scrutiny and uproar over how university police and the local district attorney’s office handled the matter two years ago. Hochul said in a statement that “newly released information continues to raise serious questions about the investigation,” which has in turn “undercut my faith, and the public’s faith.” She said James, who has been attorney general since 2019, will take over the case of a former Cornell University student who alleged in a lawsuit last month that she was raped, sexually assaulted and plied with drugs by members of Chi Phi fraternity in 2024. The student made a report to Cornell police about three weeks after the incident she alleges, and the matter was investigated by the Tompkins County district attorney, who said he found “insufficient evidence to support criminal charges” at the time. This week, District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said his office will look at the case again, but he defended its initial decision, saying the woman’s statement to police in 2024 “described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual.” The woman, identified only as Jane Doe, sued the university, seven Chi Phi fraternity brothers and other defendants on Sept. 16. None of the seven was criminally charged. The Chi Phi national fraternity said in a statement Sept. 18 that it could not discuss specific allegations during pending litigation. It called the allegations “deeply concerning,” and its local chapter has been barred from campus. “As special prosecutor, the Attorney General will investigate this incident and, if warranted, prosecute any offenses arising from that investigation and present evidence to a grand jury,” Hochul said. She said Jane Doe “deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued.” “This action will ensure that the matter is fully and thoroughly investigated without conflict or bias, and handled independently with the rigor that this matter demands,” she said. Doe’s attorney, Thomas Guiffra, praised James’ appointment Thursday, saying he and Doe “had no faith in DA Van Houten’s ability or desire to actively investigate and prosecute this case.” “We were dismayed that shortly after we agreed to give him all the assistance he needed, he published an announcement which questioned whether a crime was committed,” Guiffra said. “The most recent disclosure when he claimed that he never reviewed the transcript where Ms. Doe said “I am 100% certain I was raped” was the last straw.” Guiffra’s remark was an apparent reference to the transcript of Doe’s interview with campus police in 2024, which was reported by CBS News earlier this week. Van Houten told NBC News on Wednesday that that specific allegation was not in the written statement his office received from Cornell police at the time. NBC News has not reviewed that transcript. Guiffra said he intended to write a letter to Hochul requesting she appoint a special prosecutor, and said he and Doe “look forward to working with Attorney General James to finally obtain justice.” James said in a statement Thursday evening: “Every New Yorker deserves to know that when they report a crime, it will be investigated fully and fairly. The Governor has entrusted my office with this investigation, and we do not take that responsibility lightly.” “I stand ready to lead a process New Yorkers can trust, guided by the facts and the law,” she added. The university confirmed Wednesday that it agreed to Hochul’s call for an independent investigation, and it backed James’ appointment Thursday night. “Cornell supports Governor Hochul’s decision to assign this case to the New York Attorney General’s Office,” the university said in a statement. Van Houten did not immediately respond Thursday night to emailed requests for comment.

articles.title: Hasan Piker vows he will pressure James Talarico to govern as a leftist, not a moderate
articles.summary: Hasan Piker vowed to pressure James Talarico to govern as a leftist if elected, not a moderate Democrat, raising questions about the Texas Senate race.
articles.body: Left-wing streamer Hasan Piker vowed Wednesday that he would push Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico to govern as a leftist rather than a moderate Democrat if Talarico was elected. "Hopefully, after James Talarico wins, we’ve got to hold him to account," Piker said during a campus event at the University of Texas at Austin. "We've got to make sure that he doesn’t become another, ‘do nothing Democrat’ ‘business as usual,’ and we've got to keep up that pressure. "We have to remind him that we are the force that backed him both early on," he continued. "We are the force that allowed him to win this seat of power and if he wants to maintain it, he’s got to play ball. Right? "And that’s good to build a resilient movement anyway, so job’s not done even after he wins," Piker added. "So, just remember that, and, you know, remember that we do hold a lot of power in mass organizing." UNIVERSITY EVENT WITH HASAN PIKER IN TEXAS DRAWS BACKLASH FROM BOTH SIDES OF THE AISLE Fox News Digital reached out to Talarico's campaign for comment but did not immediately receive a response. Talarico has moderated his rhetoric during his run for Senate, disavowing some of his past statements. Piker, an internet personality popular on the Twitch platform, has become a major player in left-wing politics in recent years and has a long history of controversial comments, ranging from saying "America deserved 9/11" to praising an official in New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration after a clip showed her saying she wanted to "impoverish the White middle class." Proximity to Piker has been a lightning rod for Democrats. Since the left-wing streamer appeared with Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed on the campaign trail, the candidate repeatedly tried to shrug off Piker’s controversial remarks. TALARICO’S ‘PROUD CAPITALIST’ ABOUT-FACE COLLIDES WITH RESURFACED CALL TO ‘DISMANTLE’ CAPITALISM Jesse Arm, a Manhattan Institute vice president and pollster from Michigan, wondered whether Talarico’s avowed moderation will stick. "Talarico is wise to acknowledge, in effect, that many of his past comments on key policy questions were absurd, but Texans have reason to wonder whether his convictions have changed or merely his political incentives," he told Fox News Digital. "If he is as wise a lawmaker as he is a crafty politician, he will govern as the more moderate liberal he currently purports to be. "Hasan Piker’s faction can certainly exert pressure," he added. "And I would expect it to push Talarico back toward his earlier, more radical positions on policing, gender, race, immigration and energy." A better indicator, he argued, was the fact that genuinely moderate Democrats have been driven out of office. "We cannot know how Talarico would govern, but the broader Democratic Party gives us plenty of reason for skepticism: Joe Manchin and Kyrsten Sinema were driven out, and John Fetterman faces endless hostility for breaking with its activist orthodoxy," he said. "Governing as a genuine moderate would give Talarico a better chance of keeping a Texas Senate seat beyond an unusually favorable Democratic election cycle, but Piker is already openly demanding that he ‘play ball’ with the far left." Arm suggested Piker might actually be making a tactical mistake by suggesting Democrats are only campaigning as moderates but will govern like leftists. "Above perhaps all else, this episode exposes Piker’s political stupidity: publicly suggesting that a candidate’s moderation is temporary and that radicals will call the shots threatens the very victory he claims to want," Arm said. "In truth, I suspect Piker would prefer an election cycle in which Talarico comes up short, but El-Sayed gets across the finish line. That would help advance Piker’s position that radicalism is the only viable path forward for the Democratic Party." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Former Democratic advisor Dan Turrentine suggested Piker has vastly overestimated his importance both now and after the election. "Hasan Piker is living in fantasy world," he said. "He did not elect Talarico in the primary. Progressives were split, with many going for Jasmine Crockett. "If Talarico wins the general, it will be because he appealed to a significant number of R’s in a state Trump won by 14% in ’24," Turrentine continued. "If Talarico wins, it will be in spite of Piker, not because of him. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Same, if they win, for Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Josh Turek in Iowa, Mary Peltola in Arkansas, and Sherrod Brown in Ohio," he added. "The Senate majority runs through the middle of the electorate, not Twitch."

articles.title: NTSB report says pilots weren’t warned about wind before Amazon-branded plane crashed in Miami
articles.summary: The preliminary report didn’t list a cause of the crash. The investigation could take more than a year to complete.
articles.body: Despite regulations requiring it, an air traffic controller failed to tell the pilots of an Amazon-branded cargo plane about the potential for strong tail winds as they landed in Miami, where the plane careened off the runway and killed five people last month, according to a preliminary report Thursday from the National Transportation Safety Board. Just four minutes before clearing the plane for landing, an air traffic controller had provided a wind advisory to a different flight, noting gusts of up to 25 mph from the south. But the controller “did not issue information about the wind” to the pilots of the cargo plane, the report said. According to federal regulations, “both wind direction and velocity were required to be stated when authorizing use of a runway when a tail wind component exists,” the NTSB report said. The preliminary report did not list a cause of the crash. The ongoing investigation could take more than a year to complete. The airplane, carrying packages of contact lenses for Amazon, came in fast after a flight from Puerto Rico and barreled roughly 1,200 feet past the end of the runway at Miami International Airport on Sept. 6. It smashed into a van carrying workers for a company that cleans airplanes. Five people who were in the van died. Two others in the van sustained serious injuries, as did the driver of a car that was hit by the plane. The two pilots had minor injuries. Tail winds can make landing a plane harder Experts said it appears the weather played at least some role in the accident. Tail winds can make it harder to slow a plane and push it past an ideal landing spot on a runway. “When you’ve got winds like that, it is your responsibility as a controller to issue that to a pilot, especially on landing and especially when you have gusts,” said Tony Mello, a former Federal Aviation Administration official who oversaw air traffic control services in the central U.S. Landing with a gusting tail wind “requires more concentration on the part of the pilot” but is not impossible, said former NTSB member John Goglia. Failing to share the wind conditions “was a significant omission but, in and of itself, would not have caused a crash,” Goglia said. “Every crash is a chain of events. That’s just one event.” The plane had little runway left when it touched down A summary of cockpit voice recordings previously released by the NTSB said one of the pilots repeatedly warned his counterpart that they were going too fast as they approached for landing and after touchdown. But the fellow pilot never gave “a consistent verbal response” to the warnings, the NTSB said. The two pilots had flown together for the first time just earlier that day, according to the preliminary NTSB report. The cockpit audio recordings also captured a series of automated warnings from the plane about the speed of descent and the approaching terrain. When it touched down, the plane was traveling at 184 mph and was already about three-quarters of a mile past the start of the runway, the NTSB report said. The pilots may have tried too late to abort the landing. Data from the plane show its wheel brakes were applied, then released as the engines throttled to “go-around” thrust values before the brakes again were applied with about 415 feet of runway remaining. The plane ran off the pavement while still traveling at 130 mph, then struck some airport equipment and the cleaning crew’s van before crashing through a perimeter fence, hitting a car on a public road and coming to rest with its nose in a parking lot fence, the preliminary report said. Plane’s operator says it’s focused on safety After the crash, Amazon suspended its partnership with 21 Air, which operated the plane. The North Carolina carrier had flown packages for Amazon since 2024. The Boeing 767 that crashed was 32 years old and originally built to carry passengers. It was converted to a cargo plane in June 2016, the preliminary NTSB report said. The plane’s operator, 21 Air, said in a written statement Thursday that safety is “a core focus” of its organization. “We are reviewing the information in the NTSB preliminary report closely, alongside our own internal safety and operational protocols, and we will take all appropriate action to improve our safety based on the facts as they are established,” the company said. The Miami crash came less than a year after a UPS cargo plane crashed at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway. That crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured.

articles.title: Trump says US may ask Europe to release diesel reserves
articles.summary: Skyrocketing diesel prices have pushed Washington to weigh an export ban, raising alarm across European economies.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has said that the US could ask European countries to release diesel reserves, as Washington tries to rein in rising diesel prices due to the war on Iran.

The US president told reporters on Thursday that his administration “may” ask European countries to release diesel stocks, shortly after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged Europe to “immediately” tap its reserves.

“Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions,” Bessent said in a social media post.

Earlier, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that he believes France, Germany and Italy “would love to have a ⁠⁠⁠⁠cooperative path forward with the ⁠⁠⁠⁠United States on ⁠⁠⁠⁠how we get more diesel to market”.

European capitals have spent Thursday coordinating diesel measures, while US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said he was “highly confident” Europe could help ease soaring global prices by releasing emergency diesel inventories. ⁠⁠

US diesel prices have surged, hitting a record of $6.53 ⁠⁠⁠⁠per gallon a week ago, as data published by the European Commission showed 12 EU member states had recorded new all-time highs, including Italy, Belgium, Romania and Poland.

The spike in US diesel prices prompted the Trump administration and Republican lawmakers to consider restricting US diesel exports ahead of upcoming midterm elections.

France and Germany hold more than a third of the EU’s strategic diesel reserves, according to the Reuters news agency. EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic said a US ban on diesel would be “unexpected” but would have detrimental effects on Europe’s economy.

articles.title: NY governor appoints special counsel in Cornell frat rape investigation
articles.summary: The governor said she'd lost faith in prosecutors overseeing the case and handed it over to New York Attorney General Letitia James.
articles.body:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state's attorney general as a special prosecutor in investigating the alleged gang rape of a woman at Cornell University.

The woman has alleged she was drugged and raped by several men at a fraternity house. The case, which stems back to 2024, was reopened after the woman filed a civil lawsuit last month that thrust the allegations into the national spotlight.

"New information has raised serious questions about how this case was handled, and I've lost faith in the Tompkins County DA's ability to fairly oversee it," Hochul said.

Hochul's announcement removes Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten from overseeing the case.

The BBC has contacted Van Houten's office.

He has defended his office's previous decision not to file charges in the case, arguing they were not given enough evidence to meet the legal threshold.

Van Houten reopened the case after the civil lawsuit and said much of the information released in recent weeks about the case was not passed to his office.

"The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued," Hochul said in a statement.

The attorney general will, if warranted, prosecute any offences found by her investigation and present evidence to a grand jury, the governor said.

Letitia James, the state's chief legal officer, said on X that she stood ready "to lead a process guided by the facts and the law".

"The Governor has entrusted my office with this investigation, and we do not take that responsibility lightly," James added.

Hochul and James are scheduled to provide an update on the investigation on Friday morning local time.

The woman at the centre of the case, identified anonymously as Jane Doe in court documents, filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university in September.

She alleged that she was drugged and raped by seven men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024.

She claimed that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men, who have now become known as the Cornell Seven.

The case was initially referred to Van Houten, the top prosecutor in the county, in 2024.

Van Houten said his office did not bring charges at the time because he had only seen a statement from Doe implying the incident was consensual and that she had not been drugged.

This week, his office announced it would be reopening the case - less than two weeks after Doe filed her civil lawsuit.

Cornell has said it provided evidence to the district attorney's office from its own investigation, including a Snapchat group chat in which fraternity members discussed a "free" sexual encounter with Doe on the night of the alleged assault.

Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, has accused the district attorney of repeatedly changing his story amid news coverage of the case.

articles.title: Lawyers, experts urge Tennessee governor to commute Christa Pike’s sentence after botched execution
articles.summary: Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital in a botched Tennessee execution, and her lawyers now urge Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence.
articles.body: Christa Pike's lawyers are calling on Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life in prison after she remained alive following two doses of lethal injection drugs in what one death penalty expert described as an unprecedented event. Pike, who was sentenced to death for a 1995 murder of a classmate, was rushed to a hospital Wednesday night after surviving her planned execution. Her lawyers said on Thursday that she remains in critical condition and is receiving "lifesaving medical care." "We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment," attorney Randy Spivey said during a news conference. "But we know she is alive right now." The botched execution prompted Lee to halt any further efforts to carry out Pike's execution and the state’s other execution scheduled this year. He also ordered a third-party review into Pike's execution, which he called "deeply disturbing." CHRISTA PIKE'S ATTORNEYS SAY SHE'S IN CRITICAL CONDITION AFTER BOTCHED LETHAL INJECTIONS Pike's lawyers are now calling for her death sentence to be commuted. Her lawyers filed an emergency motion with the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, noting that she was in "unnecessary agony" and arguing that putting her through another attempted execution violated her right to be put to death without cruel and unusual punishment. Death Penalty Information Center Executive Director Robin Maher, who called the failed execution "completely unprecedented," also urged the governor to commute Pike's sentence. "Given the experience that Christa Pike went through last night, after a childhood and young adulthood that was full of gender based violence and abuse, it would be irresponsible for state officials to put her through another attempt at execution. I really hope that in light of what she's experienced, that the governor will decide to commute her sentence to a life in prison and not put her through another torturous experience in the execution chamber," Maher told Fox News Digital. Before the planned execution, about 25,000 people had signed a petition to Lee asking him to commute Pike's death sentence to life in prison. An appeals court had halted her execution early on Wednesday, but the U.S. Supreme Court overturned that stay hours later to clear the way for her to be put to death. Pike, 50, would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. She would have been the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year, driven largely by Florida's record increase in inmates put to death since 2025. Since the Supreme Court resumed the death penalty in 1976, only 18 women have been executed in the U.S., making up about 1% of all executions in the country. This was the second time this year that Tennessee had a failed execution. In May, Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was not executed because officials could not find a suitable vein for an IV line, so the drugs were not administered. Multiple states have previously paused executions after cases of officials being unable to find a suitable vein for an IV line. In 2024, Tennessee switched from a three-drug series to a single drug, pentobarbital, for lethal injections. About two years earlier, the state abruptly halted the execution of Oscar Smith, who was convicted of first-degree murder, and acknowledged it had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs had been tested properly. He was eventually put to death by lethal injection last year. Several others have survived medical problems linked to a failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one had stayed alive after receiving the drugs until Pike on Wednesday. "This, unfortunately, is not the first time that Tennessee officials have botched an execution. There is really a quite shameful history in Tennessee of executions going wrong, although Christa Pikes really stands out. There's never been someone who has received lethal doses of execution drugs and survived until last night. This is a completely unprecedented event, even in the context of Tennessee's other botched executions," Maher said. The Death Penalty Information Center lists 65 botched executions across the U.S. in the modern era. In the execution chamber, Pike said she was at peace and "ready to be free." "This is a happy day," she said. But she remained awake, and even complained about a feeling in her arm. Witnesses reported that Pike complained of pain in her arm and remained conscious after the first dose. An hour after officials first raised the curtains, witnesses said that a second dose of pentobarbital was administered. Pike could still be heard snoring behind a closed curtain until the microphone was cut off nearly 30 minutes later. Shipp was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole, as he was a minor and not eligible for the death penalty. The third defendant, then-18-year-old Shadolla Peterson, who acted as a lookout while her two friends carried out the attack, testified for the state and avoided the death penalty. articles.title: Row between Ukraine, South Korea mounts over North Korean POWs
articles.summary: South Korea’s ⁠President accused Ukraine of ⁠undermining him by disclosing POW transfer deal
articles.body:
South Korea’s ⁠President ⁠Lee Jae Myung has expressed anger at Ukraine over comments by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a speech at the UN which appeared to reveal a secret deal by which Kyiv would transfer North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul.

In a social media post on Friday, Lee accused Ukraine of undermining him and ⁠warned that Zelenskyy’s ⁠remarks about an imminent military clash between North and South Korea ‌amounted to invoking the risk of war on ‌the ‌Korean Peninsula.

The diplomatic row pits two US-aligned states with powerful militaries against each other, potentially complicating US efforts to shore up a united global front to contain Russia, China and North Korea.

The South Korean president also expressed ⁠regret over Ukraine’s response and called on Kyiv to acknowledge the agreement and apologise.

“This is a matter concerning the honor of the Republic of Korea’s people and nation, we cannot overlook it,” Lee said.

Lee also referred to an interview with Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha published by RBC-Ukraine and other Ukrainian outlets on Thursday which sought to reduce bilateral tensions.

Sybiha had said he would “not like to call it an incident”, describing it instead as a “diplomatic misunderstanding”.

“South Korea is an important country for us. And I very much hope for momentum, continued cooperation, and concrete results that we are indeed achieving with them,” he said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said during the UN General Assembly that Kyiv had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea after they were caught fighting for Russia in the Kursk region.

South Korea demanded an official apology and explanation from Ukraine, accusing Kyiv of disclosing the transfer of the two North Korean POWs to Seoul.

South Korea’s senior presidential secretary Seong Ghi-hong said in a statement that Ukraine had repeatedly discussed the prisoners’ transfer with Seoul through various channels and had requested secrecy. However, Kyiv has said no secrecy agreement existed.

articles.title: Seoul warns 'further action' if Ukraine does not apologise over prisoner-of-war row
articles.summary: President Lee Jae Myung also accused Kyiv of "attempting to provoke a war on the Korean Peninsula".
articles.body:
South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung has threatened to take unspecified "further action" if Ukraine does not issue a public apology for revealing that two North Korean prisoners of war had been sent to the South.

Ukraine's leader Volodymyr Zelensky made the disclosure to the UN general assembly last week, angering Seoul, who said the move was meant to stay secret.

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on Thursday described the situation as a "diplomatic misunderstanding", adding that Kyiv was "working" to resolve it.

Lee rejected this characterisation on X, saying it concerned "the dignity of the Korean people and the nation".

Lee's office said last week that it was Ukraine that requested for the move to be kept secret, partly to protect the North Koreans' families, and also because Kyiv wanted to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.

Zelensky's office responded, saying the two countries had no such agreement to keep the move confidential, further escalating the situation.

Lee himself faced heavy criticism at home after Zelensky's disclosure, with the South Korean opposition accusing him of covering up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.

The two soldiers, who were among thousands of North Koreans supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.

Speaking to Ukrainian media on Thursday, Sybiha, the foreign minister, said he "hopes that this situation will be resolved in the very near future".

"We are working on it. For us, South Korea is an important country. And I really hope for momentum, continuation, and concrete results that we are truly achieving with them," he said.

Lee, in response, accused Kyiv of attempting to "bring war on the Korean Peninsula".

"We express serious regret that, instead of acknowledging the facts of the agreement and apologising, they are talking about an imminent military clash between the North and South," he said in an X post.

Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has adhered to its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.

articles.title: US to send third aircraft carrier towards Iran: US official to Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Massive US military deployment to the Middle East includes 50,000 troops, F-35s and Marines to pressure Tehran.
articles.body:
The United States is deploying a third US aircraft carrier to the waters around Iran, a US official told Al Jazeera, as the war enters its eighth month and both sides weigh escalation and diplomatic engagement.

The official told Al Jazeera that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group left its San Diego base on Sunday, bound for the region, followed a day later by the Makin Island Marine Expeditionary Force, carrying more than 2,000 Marines.

By the end of November, the official said, three aircraft carriers and two amphibious landing groups will be positioned around Iran.

The official said the concentration of force would hand President Donald Trump a wider menu of options if he decides to act.

Al Jazeera’s Tanya Noury, reporting from Washington, said the new deployment includes thousands of troops and extra air power, including F-35 fighter jets, layered on top of the roughly 50,000 US service members already stationed in the region.

The goal, Noury said, citing sources inside the Pentagon and White House, is to keep military options “on the table” for Trump regardless of how diplomacy unfolds, with the Pentagon not planning to withdraw any assets even if an agreement with Iran is reached. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has said forces are “ready to go” should Trump order new strikes.

Trump himself has kept the threat alive in public. He told Fox News he believes the US is “going to win the war” with Iran “very soon”, while suggesting in other remarks that a return to military action “is possible” but something he would rather not spell out before November’s midterm elections.

Washington has paired the show of force with new economic pressure , sanctioning Iran’s rail and automotive conglomerates this week, as the Treasury Department called the new measures an effort to drain what remains of Tehran’s revenue.

Parallel to the military build-up, Iran has pushed a seven-day roadmap , conveyed through Qatar, that would see it reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks in exchange for an end to the US naval blockade, sanctions relief and a regional ceasefire covering Lebanon and Yemen.

US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz told NBC the plan’s demand for frozen funds and sanctions relief was non-negotiable, noting “these aren’t just the United States’ sanctions … these are global sanctions”, and pointing to seven UN Security Council resolutions against an Iranian nuclear weapons programme.

Iran’s response, in the meantime, has been similarly two-pronged.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told NBC that Tehran was “fully prepared” to resume the war, before writing on X that “we did not come to New York to sell a war. We came to forge peace.”

Analysts say the mixed signals are deliberate.

Abas Aslani of the Center for Middle East Strategic Studies said the dispute has shifted from whether to negotiate to “who is going to abandon the primary leverage first”, while former US ambassador Richard Schmierer said Trump is caught between delaying past the midterms and the political cost of offering concessions that mirror a June deal he was already criticised for.

Nearly 70 percent of Americans now say the war has not been worth fighting , according to a new AP-NORC poll, with Trump brushing off the slide in his approval ratings by insisting “the pollsters are corrupt”.

articles.title: Move to stop charges for parents to sit by children on flights
articles.summary: The government says sitting together can currently cost a parent and child up to £104 on a return journey.
articles.body:
The government says it will ensure parents cannot be charged for sitting next to their children on planes if new powers get approval in Parliament.

UK airlines said they adhered to existing rules.

If the Civil Aviation Bill gets approved by MPs, the department for transport says it will consult on scrapping any charges for being seated next to children under the age of 14 or correcting minor errors on flight bookings.

While acknowledging most UK airlines already offer protections against hidden costs, the government said its proposed reforms would provide greater consistency across all airlines operating in the country.

Trade body Airlines UK said it was surprised to see the announcement, adding that UK airlines already allow minor name corrections free of charge. They also follow the regulator's current guidance on seating children under 12 with their accompanying adult.

The Department for Transport says an arrangement to sit together can currently cost a parent and child up to £104 on a return journey.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the proposed rule changes are part of a crackdown on the "little charges that add up" when families plan their holiday trips.

"Charging parents just to sit with their children is a rip-off, plain and simple," he added, and being "hit with a hefty fee for a simple spelling mistake on a booking form isn't right either".

The department says minor mistakes or admin tweaks, such as correcting a name on a booking form, can cost passengers up to £40.

It added that the new rules were the "latest example of the Prime Minister's series of 'everyday fixes' to tackle the irritations that make life difficult and hit people's wallets".

"Parents should not have to feel the pinch just to sit next to their child on a flight, or for amending a simple booking error," said Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander.

Rory Boland, editor of consumer magazine Which? Travel, said it was "clearly unfair to force parents and children as young as three to pay an extra fee just to sit together".

"Airlines that have separated families are putting profit ahead of passenger peace of mind," he was quoted as saying by the Press Association.

The raft of changes include a new system for sharing information on persistently disruptive passengers, which would be created with help from airlines and trade unions.

The government says that in 2025 more than 1,000 serious disruptive passenger incidents were logged by airlines, including a mid-air brawl that resulted in a flight being diverted.

Alexander said everyone deserved to travel knowing their flight would not be disrupted by "bad behaviour from a small minority".

Airlines UK said it welcomed a commitment to crack down on disruptive passengers.

The changes are set to be delivered following Royal Assent of the Civil Aviation Bill . It is understood that ministers will try to implement the changes before the start of next year's summer holidays.

articles.title: FAO official says he lost his job for criticising Israeli policies in Gaza
articles.summary: The FAO official said he was told his contract would not be renewed over an alleged breach of impartiality on Gaza.
articles.body:
A senior UN agency director has said that he lost his job because he criticised Israeli policies in Gaza.

Ben Davis, who had been Director of Rural Transformation and Gender Equality at the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), told AFP news agency on Wednesday that he was informed in July that his contract would not be renewed because he had allegedly breached impartiality rules.

He said that he was accused of organising weekly silent protests at the Rome-based organisation.

“They accused me of organising these moments of silence on the situation of starvation and famine in Gaza,” Davis said.

Davis was also criticised for a report he worked on about food availability in Gaza and humanitarian law, published in May.

“We were told to take it down,” he said. “We weren’t allowed to make any references to humanitarian law.”

FAO Director-General Qu Dongyu appeared to warn FAO staff on Tuesday that “we don’t allow you to play the game here of human rights”.

He was speaking in public comments made at the start of a filmed session on forestry.

“Of course, human rights is very important, but we have the human rights agency in Geneva,” he added. “If you want to take care, go there.

“That’s why some senior members play the political game here, I fire him … You should follow the FAO constitution … You are against staff regulations … But I’m a very soft person, I didn’t fire that many,” he said.

“I will fire more people if they are against the law,” he added.

FAO did not respond to an AFP request for comment.

Asked if he thought the director-general’s comments were about him, Davis said “absolutely”.

“He has already scolded me in public in the past for being too political.”

Davis also said he was “concerned” about the director-general’s comments on firing more people.

Hundreds of people attended the moments of silence at their height, while now there are only 30 to 40 people coming on a weekly basis, he said.

Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed over 74,000 people since October 2023, and at least 1,431 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the so-called ceasefire between Hamas and Israel was agreed upon in October 2025.

articles.title: Iran urges Iraq to lift flight ban amid US sanctions
articles.summary: Iran calls on Iraq to remove flight curbs after US sanctions, in a move that has strained bilateral ties.
articles.body:
Iran called on Iraq to lift remaining flight restrictions caused by US sanctions and fully restore normal air travel between the two countries, even after services partially resumed at one Iraqi airport earlier in the week.

In a statement on Thursday, Iran’s Foreign Ministry condemned Washington’s “illegal and inhumane” efforts to disrupt Iran’s trade and air transport through the “extraterritorial enforcement” of US sanctions, and urged Baghdad to remove the restrictions.

It said the movement of millions of Iranian and Iraqi citizens required “an independent and responsible approach” to disagreements between the two governments.

Flights between Najaf and Iran had restarted late on Monday , according to the country’s state-run Iraqi News Agency, which credited “diligent efforts” by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi with the resumption.

Iraq’s ambassador to Iran, Yasser Abdulzahra al-Hajjaj, said Baghdad had not decided to suspend Iranian flights.

Foreign ground-handling companies refused to provide services for fear of US sanctions.

Flights remained suspended at Baghdad, Erbil and Sulaimaniyah airports, forcing passengers onto land journeys of at least 12 hours and disrupting pilgrim traffic between the Shia-majority areas.

The suspensions prompted protests across Iraq, including outside Najaf airport and in Nasiriya, Karbala and Amarah, according to the Iranian news agency Press TV.

The US ban, which took effect on September 23 and targets any company doing business with Iranian airlines, has sharply cut Iran’s international air links.

Flights to and from Tehran’s Imam Khomeini international airport have fallen 42 percent, according to aviation monitor FlightRadar24, with routes to Georgia, Oman and Azerbaijan halted entirely and flights to Dubai suspended since September 23.

Flights to China have held steady, while the busiest route, to Turkiye, has fallen by only 19 percent, even as individual airlines have shifted service on and off the route.

Iraq’s government had sought a US exemption “on humanitarian grounds related to medical treatment, education, religious visits, and the interests of civilians”.

articles.title: Hurricane Rachel strengthens to a Category 3 storm off Mexico’s Pacific coast
articles.summary: Rachel’s swells are expected to generate life-threatening surf and rip-current conditions off Mexico, the National Hurricane Center warned.
articles.body: MEXICO CITY — Hurricane Rachel has been upgraded to a Category 3 storm off Mexico’s Pacific coast as northern Mexico and parts of the U.S. Southwest were reeling from flooding and damage from the remnants of Hurricane Polo earlier this week. The storm, located about 245 miles off the southern tip of Baja California, is slowly continuing westward at 3 mph and expected to strengthen in the next day before weakening this weekend, according to the National Hurricane Center. The maximum sustained winds were 120 mph Thursday afternoon. Rachel’s swells are expected to generate life-threatening surf and rip-current conditions off Mexico’s coast, the NHC warned. Mexican authorities said Thursday they remain on alert because of forecasts of very heavy rain in the states of Baja California Sur, Sinaloa and Jalisco and the possibility of landslides, rising river levels, overflowing rivers and flooding in low-lying areas. On Wednesday night, the U.S. Embassy in Mexico warned U.S. citizens in Cabos San Lucas, a popular vacation destination for Americans, of beach and port closures and deadly rip currents. The Pacific has seen an unusually busy hurricane season, which experts have attributed to El Niño, which has fueled crippling droughts in Mexico and Central America and floods in other parts of the region. In the Pacific, it has resulted in warmer waters and wind patterns that act as fodder for hurricanes. Tropical Storm Nolo continued its northwest approach away from Hawaii on Thursday, though the National Weather Service said it could strengthen into a hurricane by the weekend. Northern Mexico still reeling from Polo Parts of northern Mexico were still reeling from floods and wider destruction left by Polo. Hundreds of people remained displaced or had their homes destroyed, and at least 13 municipalities remained flooded Thursday night, according to local authorities. Lucía Vegas, who lives in the small town of Bacabachi in the border state of Sonora, said it was a miracle she survived severe flooding as it swept through her community. She, her husband and three children were left homeless. Vegas said she and her family managed to survive thanks to their dog. In the middle of the night, as the floodwaters were rising, the dog woke her by shaking water off herself, giving the family enough time to climb a ladder onto the roof of their home just minutes before it was completely flooded. “Right now, we have been left with nothing,” the 39-year-old woman said through tears. Storm remnants drench central U.S. Areas in Texas, Nebraska, Missouri and Iowa were still under flood watch Thursday afternoon as storm remnants continued to batter the region, flooding streets and neighborhoods and setting off water rescues. Wednesday was the wettest day on record for Lincoln, Nebraska, which received 6.1 inches of rainfall, according to the University of Nebraska-Lincoln Climate Office. In Omaha, which received 4.7 inches of rain Wednesday, the fire department said it responded to 80 water rescues over a three-hour period ending early Thursday. Some floodwaters reached depths of 8 feet. Schools remained open. But many buses never made it out of flooded parking lots, prompting officials to ask parents to transport their students to school. San Antonio, Texas, was under a flash-flood warning through Thursday evening, and the city urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel. More than 19,000 residents across the state were without power Thursday afternoon, according to PowerOutage.us. Videos posted on social media showed floodwaters in Texas creating waves along Interstate 35 in Denton. In Chicago, a wastewater treatment and stormwater management utility urged residents to conserve water use to prevent flooding and stormwater backup. “We encourage everyone to conserve water when possible to create more capacity in our systems,” utility President Kari K. Steele said in a statement Wednesday. In Kansas, Gov. Laura Kelly issued an emergency proclamation on Wednesday ahead of the storms that allows state resources to assist first responders in hard-hit communities.

articles.title: How Switzerland lost 20 percent of its ice in five years
articles.summary: Swiss glaciers have lost more than 5 percent of their ice, threatening the country’s alpine economy.
articles.body:
Switzerland’s glaciers are rapidly receding due to a combination of winters with too little snow and record-high temperatures across Europe this summer, scientists say. In all, one of the world’s top ski destinations has lost nearly one-fifth of its glacial ice in just five years.

In a report (PDF) published by the Swiss Glacier Monitoring Network (GLAMOS) and the Swiss Commission for Cryosphere Observation of the Swiss Academy of Sciences (SCNAT) on Thursday, researchers said Swiss glaciers lost 5.5 percent of their ice volume over the hydrologic year ending September 30, 2026, and nearly 20 percent since 2021.

Why is Switzerland, famed for its Alpine terrain and winter sports, losing its glaciers and what does this mean for the country?

In September, a GLAMOS team visited 23 glaciers in Switzerland to record end-of-summer measurements of ice melt and snow accumulation.

Visiting one glacier named Scex Rouge in the Western Swiss Alps in early September, GLAMOS chief Matthias Huss, one of the report’s researchers, told the Reuters news agency that a measuring pole, about four metres (13 feet) high, was drilled into the ice in July to provide the team with a point of reference.

“Now when we have come back here, we saw the pole was out by three metres [10ft]. So just in August and September of this year, even excluding the heatwaves of June and July, we have lost three metres of ice at an elevation of almost 3,000 metres [9,843ft],” he explained.

“This clearly indicates these conditions that we had this summer, they are just inconsistent with the survival of these small glaciers in the Alps,” he added.

Why are glaciers in Switzerland losing ice?

According to the report, the total mean thickness of individual glaciers in Switzerland has fallen by between 2.5 and four metres in 2026. At glacier tongues – narrow glacial extensions of a glacier which project from land into a body of water – it had decreased by as much as 10 metres in some places over the summer.

“We can clearly attribute the massive ice loss to the warming, and thus anthropogenic [caused by humans] climate change. The summer has been the hottest on record in Switzerland. In addition, there was little snow in winter, and therefore the glaciers were poorly protected when the heat started,” GLAMOS chief Huss told Al Jazeera.

He noted that while their measurements have indicated that the melting has affected all glaciers in Switzerland equally, the effects were most visible on smaller glaciers.

“Those shrink very quickly and sometimes even completely disappeared. Also, large glaciers lost an enormous quantity of ice, but they remain impressive,” he added.

The report’s scientists warned that the glaciers also lost a total of about 2.2 trillion litres of water (581 billion gallons) between July and September alone.

“This is more than four times the annual drinking water consumption of all Swiss households,” the report’s researchers said and warned this could impact the country’s future water supply.

Switzerland is a country known for winter sports and Alpine tourism, which depends on the glaciers. About 4 percent of the country’s entire workforce is employed in the tourism sector.

“This affects tourism and also how we perceive the mountains – they are no longer white but increasingly grey and black,” he told Al Jazeera.

He added that the water provided by glaciers is also important for the economy. “It is used to fill up hydropower lakes that produce clean energy, and supplies the biggest streams of Europe,” he said.

“We’re not yet seeing the full consequences as glaciers are still around and they contribute water when we need it. But this potential is soon being lost,” he added.

Harry Zekollari, a glaciologist and associate research professor at the Department of Water and Climate at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel, shared a similar view.

He stressed that glaciers are important natural water suppliers, as they provide water when people need it most – in summer, when it is hot and dry.

“With climate change, glaciers initially provide more water during summer as they rapidly melt. However, as glaciers become smaller, there is less ice to be melted, and as such the water supply in summer decreases. This peak in water supply has now been passed for glaciers in the European Alps, meaning that we expect glaciers to provide less and less water in the coming years,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Glacier changes can also cause natural hazards, and since most of the ice lost turns into water that reaches the oceans, the consequences of glacier loss [in Switzerland and elsewhere] will be felt for coastlines all around the globe,” he added.

Yes. According to Zekollari, in order to save as much glacier ice as possible in Switzerland, the world needs to stabilise rising temperatures as soon as possible.

“Projections for the European Alps and Swiss glaciers show that if we are able to rapidly stop emissions, we may still be able to save about one-third of their ice mass. However, in a case with strong warming, these glaciers are projected to lose more than 90 percent of their volume by 2100,” he said.

He noted that the situation is less grim globally as some glaciers in other regions are more persistent.

“However, even globally, future emissions play a big role and will decide whether we lose about 25 percent of glacier mass by 2100 – that’s the good case, with limited warming – or rather 50 percent – the bad case, with more warming,” he said.

“The losses in the longer term – past 2100 – are even larger due to the long response of glaciers, but also here it is the future warming that decides how much remains. Every 0.1 degree Celsius warming matters.”

articles.title: Travelodge review 'emotional read' for room security victim
articles.summary: Wendy Griffith says she believes security and safety at hotels is an "industry-wide problem".
articles.body:
A woman who experienced a naked man performing sex acts outside her Travelodge hotel room says a review into the chain's security was an "emotional read".

Wendy Griffith was one of dozens of people who shared their stories after the BBC revealed how a woman woke up to a man sexually assaulting her in her bed at the chain's Maidenhead branch in December 2022 after staff gave him a key card and her room number.

Griffith said she felt "sadness and frustration that women had to go through these experiences" for the review to happen and she wants lessons to be learnt across the industry.

Travelodge said it welcomes the recommendations from the report and changes have been under way since March.

Marketing consultant Griffith, from Norfolk, was staying at Travelodge London Stratford in July 2025 when she said a man started banging on her door.

She then witnessed him through the door's peephole performing sex acts.

She recalled "rising panic" over the hour as she was "essentially trapped" in the middle of the night, trying and failing "multiple times" to contact hotel staff.

With no room phone and no emergency contact number in her room, she used her mobile to try to call the Travelodge website number.

She said she was "incredibly traumatised and not able to summon help", then dialled 999 in desperation.

The man, Trevor Reece, 40, pleaded guilty to outraging public decency in September 2025.

He was sentenced by magistrates to four months of alcohol dependency treatment and ordered to pay £185 court costs and £50 compensation to his victim, which Griffith says has yet to be paid.

She subsequently discovered that during a lull in the hour she was targeted, her tormentor - who was also a hotel guest - had gone to reception and asked for a replacement room key. He was given her room number instead of his own.

A review carried out by barrister Paul Greaney KC found room intrusions were reported at nearly one in 10 Travelodge hotels this summer and no policy was in place on violence against women and girls.

Travelodge interim chief executive Ray Reidy told the BBC the company was working with the Suzy Lamplugh Trust - a personal safety charity - to develop one.

Griffith said she had found the review "quite emotional to read" and described it as "galling".

"I mean, there's validation in it, but there's also real sadness and frustration that women had to go through these experiences before the issues were taken this seriously," she said.

"It's terrible to think that it's just taken years and years for this to come to life and such serious incidences for people to realise what's been going on and how companies like Travelodge have been behaving."

The company, which is based in Thame, Oxfordshire, said in its response to the review: "Travelodge would like to unreservedly apologise again to the woman assaulted and to all guests where Travelodge has fallen short due to failures in its policies and procedures for room access security and in its response to complaints."

Griffith said prior to her ordeal, she would "regularly travel on my own".

"I treat travel now and security in particular in hotel rooms so differently," she added.

Carolyn Pearson, CEO of travel security company Maiden Voyage, said handing a room key to someone claiming to be a guest's boyfriend is an "incredibly basic" failure, but one that is "unfortunately very common across the industry".

"This is not just a Travelodge issue," she added.

Pearson said hotels "should never ever confirm whether or not a guest is staying at the hotel or not".

Dawn Brennan, CEO of women's safety charity Wise Women, said: "We would say that no one should be getting access to any rooms unless they're registered and also provide an ID.

"But even further than that considering women's safety, the hotel should have policies in place where they double check as well if it's a partner that's coming to the reception and they don't have the key."

Griffith said she believed security and safety at hotels was an "industry-wide problem" and has set up a petition calling on the government to implement minimum safety and guest security standards across all hotels in the UK.

Each hotel, or chain, will have its own security policy which staff should abide by.

Griffith said: "What has kept me speaking up about this is the fact that so many people have been affected, in particular women, and something positive has to come from these incidences.

"Change has to happen and I've said throughout a locked hotel room should mean exactly that. Locked, safe, yours.

"What I want now is for the lessons from this review to go beyond Travelodge and help create clear national standards across the hotel industry."

articles.title: 'Everyone in the Big Brother House was just crying'
articles.summary: Oxford's Charlotte Nott says "so much" happened in the Big Brother house that could not be shown on TV.
articles.body:
An 18-year-old Big Brother contestant says she achieved her dream - but appearing on the show was a challenging experience.

Charlotte Nott, who lost parts of her arms and legs to meningitis when she was two, made a memorable entrance to the house when she removed her prosthetic legs after breaking her shoe while stepping on to the stage.

But after 13 days, Nott, from Oxford, made the decision to leave after reaching her "breaking point".

Speaking to BBC Radio Oxford, she described the experience as stressful and restrictive, but said she was happy to have done it.

"Everything is out of your control. You can't even sing. If you start singing, they tell you to stop," she said.

"You have no control over anything. I think it's just taught me a lot about myself."

Nott, who had dreamed about entering the Big Brother house for most of her life, applied in the last week of auditions.

She said she had little memory of her entrance.

"You're going on the stage, and you're on the massive screen and there's like 500 people staring at you. Your adrenaline is so high that you just forget," she said.

"I've watched clips of me in there but I haven't watched it back when I walked in. I'm too scared."

She admitted the intensity of the show did get to her.

"Everyone was just crying every day," she said. "It wasn't like torture, but I think you just get used to it."

She said viewers had only seen part of what went on.

"There's so much that they haven't shown, like so many arguments, so much stuff that they couldn't even show on TV because it became too sensitive," she said.

Nott said the constant intensity eventually became too much.

"That was just my breaking point. I just thought there's no way," she said.

But she added that, overall, she had a good experience and was happy to have gone in.

"My dream was to go on it and I've gone on it," she said. "I've had a massive response, so I'm happy."

The 23rd series of Big Brother began on 13 September and is due to run for 54 days.

articles.title: The British Art show starts UK tour in Coventry
articles.summary: The British Art Show 10 opens in Coventry, before heading around the UK on tour.
articles.body:
The decision to start the 10th edition of the British Art Show (BAS) in Coventry is an important moment for the West Midlands' art scene, according to the head of an art collective in the city.

The Hayward Gallery Touring's BAS 10 show, a Chorus of Strangers, has its opening on 2 October, with displays at Warwick Arts Centre's Mead Gallery, Coventry University and the Herbert Art Gallery and Museum. It will later move on to other cities.

"This is really important because there isn't anything in Coventry which supports artists to explore visual arts," said Kyla Craig, the creative director of Art Riot Collective.

"I really feel like this show is moving through the cities and what we want to see from it is how we connect artists from the area locally that are outside London."

BAS 10 features the work of 37 artists, including that of Turner Prize winner Nnena Kalu, all curated by the cultural commentator and writer Ekow Eshun.

In 2025, Kalu, who is autistic, became the first artist with a learning disability to win the most prestigious prize in British art.

She uses graphite, pen, oil sticks and chalk in repetitive spirals on large-scale paper. as well as creating what are described as "boulders" of multi-coloured fabric, representing the relationship between her own body and physical movement and her sculptural works.

Craig said she was particularly looking forward to seeing Kalu's work, as the Art Riot Collective worked with artists who were neuro-divergent or had other disabilities.

"There's a heavy influence of access within the whole project.

"We really want to engage audiences and humans who wouldn't normally be able to get to the British art show or activities or exhibitions that are happening because of disability.

"So we've really tried to challenge some of the main venues around access and the local venues around access and what that really means."

Sarah Shalgowsky, principal curator at Warwick Arts Centre, described the event as "the biggest touring exhibition of contemporary art in the UK".

The head of the tour Brian Cass said: "Coventry has always kind of assembled something new and remarkable from fragments of broken times.

"It always felt like a very natural place to launch because that ethos of reinvention, sits at the very heart of this show, which brings very ambitious, significant narratives to our making work over the last five years in the conversation with the histories in the city."

Art Riot is part of the Coventry Art Forum , which is staging a fringe show to coincide with BAS 10 and Craig hopes both events will inspire more creators in the city.

"I do feel like there's a massive underground movement of arts," she said.

"I suppose what we're hoping with the British Art Show is that it supports and amplifies what's there. I mean, you'll see a wealth of activities that are happening, not just been put on by organisations because of the art show, but amplified."

The British Art Show 10 runs in Coventry until January 2027, before moving on to Swansea, Bristol, Sheffield and finally Newcastle Gateshead over the next two years.

articles.title: Amazon data centre near M25 approved despite environmental fears
articles.summary: Buckinghamshire Council says the economic benefits outweigh other concerns.
articles.body:
Amazon has been given the go-ahead to build a huge data centre beside the M25, despite concerns about its environmental impact.

The development will replace 17 industrial and warehouse units on the Ridgeway Distribution Centre in Iver, Buckinghamshire.

The Ivers Parish Council said the building would have a negative impact on air quality and traffic, but Buckinghamshire Council approved the plans on Monday.

Officers concluded that the need for data centres, the employment benefits and an expected reduction in vehicle movements outweighed other considerations.

The data centre's main building would be about 20 metres (65ft) high.

The 18-acre (7.3-hectare) scheme also includes a substation, water tanks, a generator yard, security fencing and parking.

The Local Democracy Reporting Service said the parish council neither supported nor objected to the application, but asked for improvements to walking routes, including the canal path, and wanted low-emission vehicles to be used during construction.

The site is in an air quality management area, and the council's environmental health team said the 27 back-up generators would produce emissions during routine testing and maintenance.

Air-quality modelling predicted a negligible effect at the locations assessed, but officers said that did not mean the development would have no impact.

A legal agreement has secured £600,382 towards projects to offset any air pollution from the site.

It also requires a plan to monitor emissions from the generators, which would primarily use hydrotreated vegetable oil, with diesel as a back-up fuel.

Officers said Amazon had also agreed to contribute £73,000 towards improvements to public rights of way.

The approval comes after Buckinghamshire Council previously rejected plans for a data centre on green belt land at the Court Lane Industrial Estate in Iver, only for the decision to be overturned by housing secretary Angela Rayner.

However, this year the government accepted it was wrong to grant planning permission for a data centre at the nearby Woodlands Park landfill site, after it had initially been rejected by the authority.

On the latest scheme, Buckinghamshire Council said: "We don't have anything further to add."

Amazon said it would not be "sharing a statement for inclusion", but planning documents estimated the project could support 60 full-time jobs on site, alongside jobs created during construction.

articles.title: Shropshire HGV training firm 'riding out' diesel price rises
articles.summary: Fuel prices have been steadily rising since the US-Iran war began in February.
articles.body:
Record-breaking fuel prices have left a firm teaching people to drive lorries and buses having to "ride out" the rising cost of filling up its vehicles.

Prices have been steadily rising since the US-Iran war began in February. Petrol has also risen to 174.23p a litre.

Steve Dulson, managing director of Shropshire-based Dulson Training, said it was costing hundreds of pounds more to fill up each lorry compared with 2025 prices.

"Over the last 12 months we've seen a rise of up to 50p a litre, excluding VAT, and it's hard to react to that, because of how we deal with our customers," he said.

"Our customers have usually been in our pipeline for some time, taking medicals, applying for provisional [licences] or taking theory tests, so by the time they've got to their practical training, and the fuel prices have increase, they've already been quoted.

"That makes it difficult for us to put prices up."

The price of petrol and diesel had been largely falling since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.

But the war in the Middle East, which started on 28 February, has added 59p to the average cost of a litre of diesel, or just under 40%, and 41p to the price of petrol.

Supplies of diesel internationally have been heavily constrained by the conflict.

Dulson said his family-run business could find limited fuel savings by "extending breaks" during training sessions or "take routes that don't use as much fuel".

"The customer has paid us to do a job and we're going to do that to the best of our ability," he said.

"As next year comes round, we might have to increase prices to reflect what we're going through, unless there's a downturn."
